story: James Parkinson called it the shaking palsy in 1817 and noted he had studied some of his cases only by watching them in the street. His name was attached decades later by a French neurologist who thought he deserved it.

Every particle in the universe is either a boson or a fermion, and the bosons are named after Bose. Dirac chose the name. Bose himself never received a Nobel Prize, though at least ten have been awarded for work built on his.

Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with brine-soaked cloth between them and made electricity flow steadily for the first time. He demonstrated it to Napoleon, who made him a count and put him on the currency.

Ohm published his law in 1827 and German academics dismissed it as a web of naked fancies. He resigned his teaching post in disgust. Recognition came fifteen years later, from England, and eventually the unit.

Pascal built a working mechanical calculator at nineteen to help his father, a tax official, with endless sums. He also founded probability theory, largely by answering a gambler's question about how to split an interrupted bet.

A newton is roughly the weight of a medium apple in your hand — a coincidence physicists enjoy rather too much given the story about the tree. Newton himself told that story late in life, and only about seeing an apple fall.

James Joule was a brewer who did physics on the side, and he measured heat with the precision of someone used to controlling fermentation. On his honeymoon he reportedly took a thermometer to a waterfall to see if the falling water warmed up.

William Thomson realised there must be a coldest possible temperature and built a scale that starts there, so nothing is ever negative. He took his title from the river Kelvin, which ran past his Glasgow laboratory.

Michael Faraday left school at thirteen and worked as a bookbinder, reading the books he was binding. He became the finest experimentalist of the century and turned down both a knighthood and the presidency of the Royal Society.
Joseph Henry discovered electromagnetic induction before Faraday did, but he was teaching a full timetable at a small American academy and published late. Faraday got the credit; Henry got the unit.

Hertz proved radio waves exist. Asked what use they might be, he said none whatsoever — it is just an experiment that proves Maxwell was right. Within fifteen years Marconi was sending signals across the Atlantic.

Becquerel expected sunlight to make uranium salts glow, so when the weather turned cloudy he shut everything in a drawer with a photographic plate. Days later the plate was fogged anyway. He had found radioactivity by being rained off.

Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes; anyone wanting to read them must sign a waiver.

Roentgen called them X-rays because he did not know what they were. The first radiograph was of his wife's hand; she looked at her own skeleton and said she had seen her death. He refused to patent any of it.

Told as a schoolboy to add the numbers from 1 to 100, Gauss saw that they pair up into fifty sums of 101 and answered almost immediately. He went on to contribute to nearly every branch of mathematics there was.

Wilhelm Weber built a working telegraph line across Gottingen with Gauss in 1833, years before commercial telegraphy. He was later dismissed from his professorship for refusing to swear an oath to the king.

Werner von Siemens built his first telegraph business on a loan from a cousin and turned it into one of the largest electrical firms in the world. The unit of conductance is the reciprocal of the ohm — and it used to be called the mho.

Rudolf Diesel designed an engine that ignites fuel by compression alone, with no spark. In 1913 he boarded a ferry across the English Channel and was never seen again; his body was found floating ten days later.

mean: Elevator brand that became synonymous with elevators
story: Elisha Otis did not invent the elevator — he invented the brake that catches it. At the 1854 World's Fair he had himself hoisted up, then ordered the rope cut. The platform dropped a few inches and stopped.
Samuel Colt is said to have got the idea for the revolving cylinder watching a ship's wheel lock into position as it turned. He carved his first model out of wood on that voyage, aged sixteen.

The rifle made the family fortune. Sarah Winchester, the widowed heir, spent decades adding rooms to a California mansion — stairs to nowhere, doors opening onto walls — in a house that still stands and can still be visited.
Henry Deringer spelled his name with one r. Rival manufacturers copying his pocket pistol added a second to dodge the trademark, and the misspelling is the version that survived into the dictionary.

The Family Shakespeare removed everything Thomas Bowdler thought unsuitable to read aloud. His sister Henrietta did most of the editing but published anonymously, so the brother's name became the word for censoring a text.

Franz Mesmer claimed to heal patients by redirecting an invisible fluid he called animal magnetism. A royal commission including Benjamin Franklin investigated and found no fluid — but noticed the patients often got better anyway.

Jean Nicot was a French ambassador who sent tobacco seeds to the queen as a headache remedy. The plant, the genus and the addictive chemical inside it all ended up carrying the name of a diplomat who never smoked.

Linnaeus named the whole tobacco genus after Jean Nicot. It is a large family — tobacco's relatives include the tomato, the potato, the aubergine and deadly nightshade, all in the same botanical clan.

Named for Anders Dahl, a Swedish student of Linnaeus. The tubers were brought from Mexico to Europe partly as a possible food crop to replace the potato. Nobody liked the taste, so it was kept for the flowers.

Leonhart Fuchs died in 1566, nearly two centuries before the flower was found and named for him. The colour is named after the flower, so a sixteenth-century German doctor is the reason a shade of pink has that spelling.

Pierre Magnol invented the idea of the plant family — grouping species by shared structure rather than listing them alphabetically. Magnolias themselves are older than bees, and are pollinated by beetles instead.

Alexander Garden was a Scottish-born naturalist working in Charleston who sent specimens back to Europe for years. He was rewarded with a flower he had nothing to do with discovering — and which does not grow where he lived.

Georg Kamel was a Jesuit missionary and pharmacist in the Philippines. Linnaeus latinised his name to Camellus for the flower. Tea comes from the same genus, so every cup you drink is technically a camellia.

Michel Begon was a French colonial governor who collected plants and sponsored botanists. He never saw the flower named after him — it was named by a monk he had once employed, years after Begon's death.

Joel Poinsett was the first United States minister to Mexico and sent cuttings home in 1828. The Mexican name is flor de nochebuena, Christmas Eve flower — rather better than naming it after a visiting diplomat.

William Forsyth was royal head gardener at Kensington and a founder of what became the Royal Horticultural Society. He also sold the government a tree-wound plaster that turned out not to work, which caused a considerable scandal.

Johann Gottfried Zinn was an anatomist who mapped the structures of the human eye, and died at thirty-two having also written on Mexican plants. There is a zone of the eye named after him as well as the flower.

Named for Caspar Wistar — with an a. The botanist who named it spelled it with an e, nobody corrected him, and two centuries later we all still misspell an anatomist's surname every time we mention the flower.
This one is a trap. It looks like somebody called Philo Dendron, but it is plain Greek: philo-dendron, tree-loving, because the plant climbs. Not every scientific-sounding plant name hides a person.
In 1943 Ignacio Anaya was closing up when a group of American army wives arrived hungry. He fried some tortilla, added cheese and jalapeno, and served it. Ignacio's nickname was Nacho.

Created for the ballerina Anna Pavlova during a tour, and claimed by both Australia and New Zealand ever since. A researcher combing old cookbooks found the earliest recipe in New Zealand, which has settled nothing.
American soldiers in Italy found espresso too strong and added hot water. Italian baristas named the result after them, not entirely as a compliment. It is now on the menu in Italy too.

Every origin story for the martini is contested: a town called Martinez in California, a vermouth brand called Martini and Rossi, a bartender of the same name. The drink is older than any reliable record of it.

mean: Atomic mass unit (historical); color blindness term
story: John Dalton was colour blind and wrote the first scientific description of the condition, using himself as the subject. He asked for his eyes to be examined after his death; they are still preserved in Manchester.

A rare potassium mineral found near volcanic vents on Vesuvius, named for Avogadro. It is one of the quieter honours in science — a man who waited fifty years for recognition, given a mineral almost nobody has seen.

Copernicus is said to have received the first printed copy of his book on the day he died. Moving the Sun to the centre was not only astronomy; it was the moment humanity stopped being at the centre of anything.

Pasteur was asked why French wine kept going sour. He found living organisms in it and showed that a short spell at moderate heat killed them without ruining the taste. Applied to milk, it saved a great many children.

Amelia Bloomer did not invent them — she promoted them in her newspaper, and the press attached her name. Women wearing them were mocked in the street, and the campaign was dropped as a distraction from the vote.

Named after a play. Sarah Bernhardt played Princess Fedora in 1882 wearing a soft centre-creased hat, and women adopted it as a symbol of the movement for women's rights before men took it over entirely.

John Stetson made a wide-brimmed hat on a prospecting trip to keep sun and rain off, and sold it off his own head for five dollars. He called the design the Boss of the Plains and built a factory on it.

Charles Macintosh spelled his name without the k. He glued two layers of cloth together with rubber dissolved in naphtha — a by-product of the gasworks — and made the first genuinely waterproof coat. The k crept in later.
Named for a battle, not a person. British troops at Balaclava in the Crimean winter of 1854 were sent knitted headgear from home because the army had not equipped them for the cold.

Louis Reard named his 1946 swimsuit after Bikini Atoll, where an atomic bomb had been tested four days earlier — he wanted a name that suggested an explosion. No Paris model would wear it, so he hired a dancer.

The fourth Earl of Chesterfield is said to have commissioned a sofa that would let a gentleman sit upright without creasing his suit. He is better remembered for letters of advice to his son that Samuel Johnson called immoral.

Laszlo Biro was a journalist who noticed newspaper ink dried almost instantly while his fountain pen smudged. He built a pen that used the thicker ink with a rolling ball to feed it. Britain still calls every ballpoint a biro.

Earl Tupper's airtight seal sold badly in shops because nobody could see why it mattered. Brownie Wise worked out you had to demonstrate the burp in someone's living room, and invented the Tupperware party.

Candido Jacuzzi's young son had rheumatoid arthritis and needed hydrotherapy at hospital. The family made pumps for farms, so Candido built a portable pump to put the treatment in the family bath. The spa industry came later.

Sisyphus cheated death twice — once by chaining up Death himself, so that for a while nobody on earth could die. His punishment was a boulder that always rolls back. Camus argued we must imagine him happy.

Tantalus stood in water that drained whenever he bent to drink, under fruit that swung away whenever he reached. English took his name for the very specific cruelty of something being just out of reach.
Narcissus saw his reflection in a pool, did not realise it was himself, and could not leave. The flower that grew where he died still bends its head toward water.

Oedipus was abandoned as a baby precisely so the prophecy could not come true, and it came true because he was abandoned. Freud borrowed the name in 1899 for a theory the play itself does not require.
Procrustes offered travellers a bed and guaranteed a perfect fit — by stretching anyone too short and cutting down anyone too tall. Theseus eventually gave him the same treatment on his own bed.

When Odysseus sailed for Troy he left his son with a friend named Mentor. Athena kept borrowing that shape to deliver advice — so the word for a trusted guide is really the name of a goddess's disguise.
Ten years to sail home from a war that itself took ten years. Odysseus survives by lying, hiding and outthinking everything he meets, which makes him a strange sort of hero and a very durable one.

Twelve labours, each supposedly impossible: the lion, the hydra, the stables, the golden apples. He was given them as punishment, completed all twelve, and the word for an enormous task has been his ever since.
A lion at the front, a goat rising from the back, a snake for a tail. Even the Greeks found it absurd, which is why chimera came to mean a wild impossible idea rather than an actual monster.
Three heads, so one is always awake. The way past was music — Orpheus played him to sleep — or cake, since Romans buried honey cakes with their dead specifically as a bribe. Hence a sop to Cerberus.

Janus guarded doorways, with one face looking back and one forward. His temple doors in Rome stood open in wartime and shut in peace. In roughly seven hundred years they were recorded as closed only a handful of times.

mean: Strengthen rubber with sulfur and heat
story: Charles Goodyear spent years and several fortunes trying to make rubber stable, and found the answer by accidentally dropping a rubber-and-sulphur mixture on a hot stove. He named it for the Roman god of the forge, and died in debt.
The fastest-moving planet took the name of the fastest god. The liquid metal got it too, for rolling away the moment you touch it — and gave English mercurial for anyone whose mood does the same.

mean: Relating to war or the military
story: Everything military traces to Mars: martial arts, martial law, court-martial. March is his month too, because it was when the campaigning season opened and Roman armies could move again.

Medieval doctors believed the planet overhead at your birth set your temperament. Jupiter — Jove — produced the cheerful sort. Saturn produced the gloomy sort, which is why saturnine still means what it does.

Pan was the goat-legged god of wild places, and travellers who heard an unexplained noise in an empty wood blamed him. That particular fear — sudden, irrational, contagious — is the one that kept his name.
Echo was a nymph who talked too much, and Hera cursed her to repeat only other people's last words. She fell in love with Narcissus and could never say so — only give him his own words back.

mean: Flower; colored part of the eye
story: Iris was the rainbow, and the messenger who ran along it between gods and mortals. The coloured ring of your eye is named after her, and so is the flower, and so is the word iridescent.
Flora was the Roman goddess of flowers and spring, and her festival involved so much noise and colour that stricter Romans disapproved. Biologists took her name for all the plant life of a place.
Faunus was the Roman god of forests and wild animals, and his female counterpart Fauna gave her name to all animal life. Flora and fauna are a goddess and a goddess, still working as a pair.
Hymen was the Greek god of weddings, and a hymeneal is a wedding song. Greek marriage processions called his name aloud on the way to the bride's house, which is where the word comes from.
The Romans made him a chubby child with a bow. The Greeks knew him as Eros and took him rather more seriously — a primordial force older than most of the gods, not a decoration for a card.

Erebus was darkness itself, born near the beginning of things. A British polar ship took the name, and after it was lost in the Arctic, a volcano in Antarctica was named after the ship — darkness, twice removed.
Morpheus did not bring sleep; he supplied the people who appear in your dreams, taking their shapes himself. His name comes from morphe, the Greek for form.

A German pharmacist isolated it from opium in 1804 and named it after the god of dreams. He tested it on himself and on three boys, nearly killing all four, then spent much of his life addicted to it.

Hypnos was the Greek god of sleep, brother of Death and son of Night. Hypnosis is not really sleep at all — the name was chosen before anyone understood what was happening — and its coiner later regretted it.

Thanatos was the gentle personification of death, as distinct from the violent kind. Thanatology — the study of dying, grief and how people face the end — took his name rather than a harsher one deliberately.

From Hebe, goddess of youth, because the condition was first described in adolescents. Like several psychiatric terms built from Greek gods, it has largely been retired in favour of plainer clinical language.

Mnemosyne was memory, and the mother of all nine Muses — which makes memory, in Greek thinking, the parent of every art. Sensible, for a culture that recited Homer for centuries before writing it down.
A museum was originally a place belonging to the Muses — a shrine to the nine goddesses of the arts. The greatest of them, at Alexandria, was a research institute with the famous library attached.
Music means, literally, the art of the Muses. It covered poetry and dance as well as sound, because the Greeks did not separate them — a performance was all three at once.

Hygieia was the daughter of the god of medicine, and her job was keeping people well rather than curing them once sick. Her sister Panacea handled cures — and gave English a word for a remedy for everything.

Ancient physicians claimed descent from Asclepius, god of medicine, and called themselves Asclepiads. His snake-wound staff is still the symbol of medicine — though it is often confused with a different, two-snake staff belonging to Hermes.

The Roman spelling of Asclepius. When plague struck Rome in 293 BC the Senate sent for the god, and a snake from his temple reportedly boarded the ship and slid off onto an island in the Tiber, where they built him a temple.

Hermes Trismegistus was a legendary sage credited with secret writings. Alchemists working in that tradition developed a way of fusing glass to seal a vessel completely — so a hermetic seal is named after a wizard.
Renamed for Augustus in 8 BC. The story that he stole a day from February so his month would match Julius Caesar's is a medieval invention — but the Senate really did rename it for him.
Renamed for Julius Caesar after his death, in the month he was born. He had just reformed the calendar into something close to the one we use, so the honour was at least on topic.

An old medical term for nicotine poisoning, built from the name of the French diplomat who introduced tobacco to his queen as a headache cure. He would probably not have chosen this particular memorial.

Orwell wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four in 1948 and swapped the last two digits for the title. The word now gets used for any surveillance at all, which slightly misses the point — his real subject was the corruption of language.

Darwin sat on his theory for twenty years, worried about the reaction. He only published when a letter arrived from Alfred Russel Wallace describing the same idea — and their work was presented jointly.

mean: Relating to evolution or competitive selection
story: Darwin never wrote survival of the fittest — Herbert Spencer coined it, and Darwin adopted it reluctantly in a later edition. Fittest means best-suited to the surroundings, not strongest, which is the misunderstanding that persists.

Gregor Mendel grew about 28,000 pea plants in a monastery garden and worked out the rules of inheritance. His paper was almost entirely ignored for thirty-four years, until three separate scientists rediscovered it at once.

Lamarck thought a giraffe that stretched for high leaves would pass longer necks to its young. He was wrong about the mechanism, but he was arguing that species change at all, decades before Darwin — which took some courage.

Pasteur's germ theory met fierce resistance from doctors who resented being told they carried disease on their hands. He was also a chemist, not a physician, which the medical establishment mentioned frequently.

Koch identified the bacteria behind anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera, and set out the rules for proving any such link. He and Pasteur were bitter rivals, and their national newspapers cheered them on.

Mendel's laws describe how traits pass on in neat ratios — but he chose pea characteristics that happened to be unusually simple. Most inheritance is far messier, which is partly why his results looked almost too tidy.

Linnaeus gave every living thing a two-word name, genus then species, replacing descriptions that ran to whole sentences. He also named himself: born Carl Nilsson, he took Linnaeus from a lime tree on the family farm.

Cuvier could reconstruct an entire animal from a few bones, and proved that species go extinct — an idea many found impossible, since it implied the creation was not perfect. He rejected evolution to his last day.
Buffon estimated the Earth was at least 75,000 years old by heating iron spheres and timing how long they took to cool. The Church objected. He apologised in print and went on believing it.

A Freudian slip is a mistake that supposedly reveals a hidden thought. Freud's own term was Fehlleistung — faulty achievement — and he collected examples obsessively, including a great many of his own.
Jung was Freud's chosen successor until they fell out permanently over how much of the mind is sexual. He went on to argue that certain images recur across all cultures, and called them archetypes.

Adler broke with Freud over the same question and built a psychology around the drive to overcome feelings of inferiority. He gave us inferiority complex, one of the few psychiatric terms everyone uses correctly.

Pavlov was studying digestion, not learning, and the dogs' drooling was ruining his measurements. He investigated the nuisance instead of eliminating it, and found conditioning. He was not, incidentally, ringing a bell — usually a metronome.

Skinner trained pigeons to guide missiles during the Second World War, and the system worked — the military just could not bring itself to trust it. He also raised his daughter's early months in a heated, filtered climate-controlled crib.

Piaget worked out his stages of child development largely by watching his own three children very closely and writing down everything. He published his first scientific paper, on an albino sparrow, at the age of eleven.

Maslow never drew his hierarchy as a pyramid — someone else added that later, and the shape implies a rigidity he did not intend. He was interested in what healthy people do, when psychology mostly studied illness.

Descartes is supposed to have thought of coordinates while lying in bed watching a fly on the ceiling and wondering how to describe its position with numbers. Every graph you have ever drawn descends from that fly.

Platonic love, in Plato, meant a love that climbs from a particular person toward beauty and truth themselves. English flattened it into love without romance, which Plato would have considered the least interesting part.

Aristotle tutored Alexander the Great, dissected sea creatures on Lesbos, and wrote the first surviving works on logic, physics and drama. For much of the Middle Ages, scholars simply called him The Philosopher.

Socrates wrote nothing. Everything we have comes from students, chiefly Plato. His method was to ask questions until the other person discovered their own answer had a hole in it — which made him popular with the young and not with anyone else.

mean: Lover of fine food and pleasure
story: Epicurus taught that the greatest pleasure is freedom from pain and anxiety, and lived on bread, water and the occasional pot of cheese. English turned his name into a word for a gourmet, which reverses him completely.
Named after a building. Zeno taught on a painted porch — a stoa — in Athens, and his followers were called the porch people. Their doctrine was that you control your judgements and nothing else.

From the Greek for dog-like. The Cynics lived rough on purpose, and Diogenes is supposed to have accepted the insult and adopted it. Modern cynicism — assuming bad motives — is a long way from the original.
Euclid's Elements ran as a school textbook for over two thousand years — the longest run of any book but the Bible. Asked by a king for a shortcut, he replied that there is no royal road to geometry.

Pythagoras ran what was half a school and half a secret society, with rules against eating beans. The theorem was known to Babylonian mathematicians a thousand years earlier; his followers may have supplied the first proof.

Archimedes worked out how to measure the volume of a crown in the bath and, the story goes, ran into the street shouting. He was killed by a Roman soldier while drawing diagrams in the sand, reportedly telling him not to disturb them.

The bell curve turns up everywhere — heights, errors, exam marks — because adding up enough small independent effects produces it almost regardless of what those effects are. Gauss found it while analysing astronomical errors.

George Boole reduced logic to algebra with two values, true and false, in 1854. He thought he was studying the laws of thought. Ninety years later it turned out he had written the mathematics of every computer ever built.

Fibonacci's real service to Europe was not the sequence but the digits: he brought Hindu-Arabic numerals west in 1202, and argued they beat Roman numerals for arithmetic. The rabbits were a small example in a long book.

Euler went blind in his sixties and his output actually increased — he dictated to his sons. He produced so much that a project to publish his complete works has been running since 1911 and is still not finished.

Asked by Napoleon why his book on the heavens never mentioned God, Laplace is said to have replied that he had no need of that hypothesis. The operator named after him turns up in heat flow, waves and quantum mechanics.
Keynes argued governments should spend in a downturn rather than tighten their belts. Told that markets would correct themselves eventually, he replied that in the long run we are all dead.

Ricardo showed two countries both gain from trade even when one is better at making everything — each should do what it gives up least to make. It is counterintuitive enough that people still argue against it two centuries on.

Malthus predicted population would outrun the food supply and reasoned it could only end in famine. He did not foresee fertiliser, mechanised farming or falling birth rates — so he was wrong, and influential anyway.
Marxian points at the analysis; Marxist points at the politics. Economists who use his tools to study capitalism without wanting to overthrow it tend to insist on the first word.
Marx spent his most productive years in the Reading Room of the British Museum, in poverty, supported largely by Engels. He is buried in Highgate Cemetery in London, a short walk from where he wrote.

Lenin argued a revolution needed a small disciplined party to lead it rather than waiting for the workers to rise on their own. He returned to Russia in 1917 in a sealed train, permitted through Germany by an enemy hoping to destabilise Russia.

Stalin was a name he chose — it means man of steel. He was born Ioseb Jughashvili in Georgia and trained briefly as a priest. His rule is associated with forced collectivisation and mass political repression.

Mao adapted a theory built for industrial workers to a country that was overwhelmingly rural, arguing revolution would come from the peasantry. It was a substantial departure from what Marx had written.

Trotsky organised the Red Army, lost the power struggle after Lenin's death, and was exiled. He was killed in Mexico in 1940 by an assassin with an ice axe, while his followers argued for permanent revolution.

Gandhi's satyagraha meant refusing to cooperate with injustice while refusing to answer it with violence. In 1930 he walked 240 miles to the sea to make salt, breaking a British monopoly with a handful of mud.

Britain's first woman prime minister and its longest-serving of the twentieth century. Her programme of privatisation and deregulation still divides the country, which is why the word gets used as praise and insult in equal measure.
The argument that cutting taxes at the top increases total revenue by growing the economy. A journalist coined the word on air; the administration disliked it at first and then adopted it.

Rule by a strong leader who claims to speak directly for the people, over the heads of parliaments. Napoleon held plebiscites to confirm his power, which made his authority look popular and left nobody able to challenge it.

Bismarck unified Germany through what he called blood and iron, then introduced the world's first national health insurance and old-age pensions — partly to undercut the socialists. Ruthlessness and welfare, from the same man.

Not merely bureaucratic — Kafkaesque means the system is impossible to argue with because nobody in it will admit to being in charge. Kafka asked his friend to burn all his manuscripts. His friend published them instead.

Dickens was twelve when his father went to debtors' prison and he was sent to paste labels on bottles in a factory. He told almost nobody for the rest of his life, and wrote about it in every book he produced.

Shakespeare is the first recorded user of something like 1,700 English words — though first recorded often means only that his plays survived and the pamphlets did not. Either way, he was not shy about inventing one.

We do not know whether Homer was one person, several, or a tradition. The poems were composed to be recited from memory, and their repeated phrases — swift-footed Achilles, the wine-dark sea — are the scaffolding that made that possible.

Milton went completely blind in his forties and composed Paradise Lost at night in his head, dictating each morning to whoever was available. Twelve books of epic verse, and he never saw a line of it written down.
Chaucer wrote in English when serious writers used Latin or French, and largely settled which English would become standard. He also held a day job as a customs official on the London docks.

In A Modest Proposal, Swift suggested in flat reasonable prose that the Irish poor should sell their children as food. Readers who missed the satire were exactly the point — he was mimicking the economists of his day.

Brooding, brilliant, self-destructive and impossible to advise. Byron largely invented the type by living it; a former lover called him mad, bad and dangerous to know, and the phrase has followed him for two centuries.

Curiously, the word is pronounced quick-SOT-ic in English while the character is Key-HO-tay in Spanish — the adjective went one way and the name the other. Both mean chasing something noble and impossible.
Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in six weeks because he needed money, and published it himself. It has never been out of print, and Scrooge's name became the word for a miser within a few years.

Pollyanna plays the glad game: find something to be pleased about in any disaster. The book was a bestseller in 1913, and her name turned into a mild insult for optimism that refuses to look at facts.
From a 1703 play, The Fair Penitent, where Lothario seduces and abandons the heroine. He is on stage for a fraction of the play and is the only thing anybody remembers about it.

Casanova was a soldier, spy, violinist, and briefly a librarian at a Bohemian castle, which is where he wrote his memoirs out of boredom. They run to twelve volumes, and the romance is a small part of them.
Romeo is in love with a different girl, Rosaline, when the play opens, and forgets her the instant he sees Juliet. The whole tragedy takes place in about four days.

In the 1894 novel Trilby, Svengali hypnotises a tone-deaf girl into a great singer who cannot perform without him. The book was a sensation, and gave English both a word and, from a character's hat, the trilby.
Rabelais's giant Gargantua was born calling for a drink, and in one episode a whole army shelters from the rain under his tongue. He is also, in the same book, sent to school and taught rather well.

Dr Pangloss insists this is the best of all possible worlds while being hanged, dissected and enslaved in succession. Voltaire was mocking a real philosophical position, and did such a thorough job that the name became the argument against it.

Conan Doyle modelled Holmes on his medical teacher Joseph Bell, who could deduce a patient's trade and travels before they spoke. Doyle killed Holmes off at a waterfall and public outrage forced him to bring him back.
A Watsonian explanation stays inside the story — Watson made a mistake in his notes. A Doylist one steps outside it — Conan Doyle forgot. Fans of every fictional world now use both terms.

Moriarty appears properly in one story and is mentioned in a handful of others. Conan Doyle invented him specifically as someone impressive enough to kill Holmes off with, and he has loomed over the canon ever since.
Without a strong state, Hobbes wrote, life would be solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short. He was writing during the English Civil War, which rather explains the mood.

Locke argued government is legitimate only by the consent of the governed, and that people may replace one that fails them. Jefferson borrowed the structure of that argument almost directly for the Declaration of Independence.

Rousseau opened his most famous book with man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains. He also wrote a celebrated treatise on educating children while placing all five of his own in a foundling hospital.

Confucius held only minor office and considered himself a failure. His students wrote down his conversations after his death, and those notes shaped Chinese government, family life and education for two thousand years.
The Tao Te Ching opens by saying that the Way which can be named is not the true Way — a book that begins by warning you it cannot do its job. It is one of the most translated texts in the world.

Buddha is not a name but a title meaning the awakened one. Siddhartha Gautama was a prince who left the palace, saw sickness, age and death for the first time, and spent the rest of his life on what to do about them.
The book of Acts records that followers were first called Christians at Antioch — and it was probably a nickname given by outsiders rather than one they chose. They adopted it anyway.

Luther set out ninety-five points for debate in 1517 and, thanks to the new printing press, they were all over Germany within weeks. He was arguing for reform, not a new church — the split happened anyway.

Calvin turned Geneva into a model reformed city, strictly governed. The doctrine that God has already chosen the saved gave rise, oddly, to a famously hard-working culture — since worldly success might be a sign of it.

John Wesley and his Oxford friends were mocked as Methodists for the methodical way they organised their prayer and study. They adopted the insult. Wesley rode an estimated 250,000 miles on horseback preaching.

Benedict's sixth-century Rule set out how a monastery should divide the day between prayer, work and reading. It is also a liqueur — made to a recipe a wine merchant claimed to have found in an old monastic manuscript.
Dominic founded an order of travelling preachers. Latin-speaking wits nicknamed them Domini canes — the hounds of the Lord — a pun the order seems to have enjoyed, since dogs turn up in their art.

Francis of Assisi gave away his inheritance, including the clothes he was wearing, and founded an order on absolute poverty. He is said to have preached to birds, and is now the patron saint of animals and ecology.

mean: Member of the Society of Jesus
story: Ignatius Loyola was a soldier until a cannonball shattered his leg and he read the only books available during a long recovery. The order he founded became the great educational network of the Catholic world.
Augustine's Confessions is arguably the first autobiography in the Western tradition — a man examining his own mind in public. He prayed, famously, for chastity, but not yet.

Aquinas set out to reconcile Aristotle with Christian theology and produced a work of immense length. Near the end of his life he had an experience after which he stopped writing, saying everything he had written seemed like straw.

Machiavelli wrote The Prince while out of a job, partly hoping to be hired again. Within decades English playwrights had turned his name into a stock villain who smiles while calculating exactly how to use you.
Vidkun Quisling helped Germany occupy Norway in 1940, and his name became the English word for a traitor within about a week — while he was still alive to read it. He was executed in 1945.

mean: Organized refusal to deal with someone
story: Captain Boycott was a land agent in Ireland who evicted tenants in 1880. The community simply stopped dealing with him — no worker, no shop, no post. He had to import labour under police guard to save his harvest, and left.

Probably from Charles Lynch, a Virginia judge whose unofficial wartime court handed out floggings. Lynch law began as a phrase for rough frontier justice and became the name for one of America's darkest habits.

In 1812 Governor Elbridge Gerry approved a district shaped so oddly that a newspaper drew wings on it and called it a salamander. His name was hard-G — so strictly it should be gerrymander with a hard sound, which nobody says.

Etienne de Silhouette was finance minister for eight months and imposed such harsh economies that anything cheap was mocked as being a la Silhouette. Cut-paper profiles were the cheapest portraits going, and the insult stuck to them.
Samuel Maverick was a Texas rancher who did not brand his cattle. Neighbours took to calling any unbranded animal a maverick — and then any person who refuses to carry anybody's mark.

Joseph-Ignace Guillotin opposed the death penalty and proposed the machine as a humane step toward abolishing it. He was appalled to have it named after him, and his family later petitioned unsuccessfully to have the name changed.
Jules Leotard invented the flying trapeze and performed in a knitted one-piece that let the audience see the body work. He also inspired the song about the daring young man on the flying trapeze.

The seventh Earl of Cardigan led the Charge of the Light Brigade — a catastrophic order, gallantly obeyed. He came home a celebrity, and the knitted waistcoat his officers wore in the Crimea took his name.

The duke asked his shoemaker for a boot tough enough for the field and neat enough for the evening. It became so fashionable that gentlemen wore them everywhere; the rubber version arrived decades later.

Lord Raglan lost his right arm at Waterloo, and asked for his sleeve to be cut in one piece running to the collar so he could dress unaided. The design turned out to allow better movement and is now standard on sportswear.

William Hoover made leather goods. A department-store janitor named Murray Spangler built the vacuum cleaner out of a fan, a pillowcase and a broom handle — then sold the patent to Hoover, his wife's cousin.

From Greek xeros graphos, dry writing, because the process needed no liquid ink. The inventor was turned down by more than twenty companies before one took it on. Xerox now sends letters asking people not to use it as a verb.
Launched in 1924 as a disposable cloth for removing cold cream. Customers kept writing in to say they were blowing their noses on it instead, so the company changed the advertising and the market.
James Dewar invented the vacuum flask and never patented it. A German glassware firm did, ran a public competition to name it, and a resident of Munich won with thermos — Greek for hot.
Otis owned the trademark and lost it by using the word generically in its own advertising. A court ruled in 1950 that the company had turned its own brand into an ordinary noun.
Bayer's trademark, lost as a war reparation — the Treaty of Versailles handed the name to the Allies in 1919. It is still a Bayer trademark in Germany and generic in Britain and America.

The toy is thousands of years old, but the name is Filipino. Pedro Flores brought it to America in the 1920s; Donald Duncan bought his company, trademarked the word, and eventually lost the trademark for being too successful.
Students at Yale threw empty pie tins from the Frisbie Pie Company. When Wham-O started selling a plastic flying disc they heard the students shouting Frisbie, respelled it, and used it as the brand.
An English firm trademarked the sound the game makes. Everyone else had to call it table tennis, which is why the sport's governing body uses the duller name and the rest of us do not.

George de Mestral came back from a walk and looked at the burrs stuck to his dog under a microscope — tiny hooks catching in loops. He spent eight years reproducing it, and named it from velours and crochet.

Asked why the penalty for petty theft was death, Draco reportedly said small crimes deserved it and he could think of nothing worse for the large ones. Athenians said his laws were written in blood rather than ink.
Two women each claimed the same baby. Solomon called for a sword and offered them half each. One agreed; the other begged him to give the child away instead — and he handed the baby to her.
From Judah, one of the twelve tribes, whose emblem was a lion. The name travelled from the tribe to a kingdom to a Roman province, and from there into the words Judaism and Jewish.
Aaron was Moses's brother and did the talking, because Moses said he was slow of speech. The priesthood descended from him, so the family that spoke for Moses ended up speaking for everybody.

Careful — this is the Moses word, meaning of his law. The mosaic made of coloured tiles is unrelated: that one comes from the Muses, via rooms decorated in their honour. Two identical English words, two different origins.

mean: Pertaining to David or his dynasty
story: David was a shepherd boy who became king, and the line descending from him mattered enormously to later writers — both Gospel genealogies take care to route Jesus back to him.

The giant loses because David refuses to fight the way giants fight. He turns down armour, keeps his sling, and wins at a distance — which makes the story less about size than about choosing your own contest.

Job loses his family, his wealth and his health, and keeps asking why. The book never really answers him. The patience of Job is proverbial, though anyone who reads it notices he complains a great deal.
Judas gave up his teacher for thirty silver coins and marked him with a kiss so the soldiers would know which man to take. Two thousand years later, almost nobody names a child Judas.

The point of the parable is who the helper was: Samaritans and Judeans despised each other. A modern retelling would have to pick whichever group the listener likes least, which is uncomfortable, and deliberate.

Frankenstein is the scientist, not the creature — the monster has no name at all. Mary Shelley was eighteen when she wrote it, during a wet summer holiday where the group agreed to each write a ghost story.

Mercator put a picture of Atlas holding up the world on the front of his collection of maps in 1595, and the name transferred from the picture to the book. Atlas himself held up the sky, not the Earth.

Daughter of the god of medicine, and her job was keeping people well rather than curing them. Her sister Panacea handled cures. Prevention and treatment, split between two sisters, which is roughly how medicine still divides.
The gentle death, as opposed to violent death, who was his brother. Freud later borrowed the name for a supposed drive toward destruction — a use the Greeks would not have recognised at all.
The Titans were the generation of gods before the Olympians, and they lost. Naming the largest ship afloat after a family famous chiefly for being overthrown was, in hindsight, an odd choice.
Mount Olympus was where the gods lived; Olympia, where the games were held, is a different place about two hundred miles away. English uses Olympian for both the majestic sense and the athletic one.

The river was named by a Spanish explorer who reported being attacked by women warriors. The bookshop was named after the river, because its founder wanted something that suggested enormous scale and started with A.
Spartan boys left home at seven for military training and were underfed on purpose, so they would learn to steal food. A boy caught stealing was punished — not for the theft, but for being caught.

Corinth was rich, and its architecture showed it. In Victorian England a Corinthian also meant a wealthy amateur sportsman — which is why an English football club founded by gentlemen amateurs is called Corinthian.
The order with the scrolls at the top, like a ram's horns or a rolled scroll. Greek writers considered it the feminine order to the Doric's masculine — slimmer, more decorated, and set on a base.
The plain one — no base, no scrolls, just fluting and a flat top. The Parthenon is Doric. It is the oldest of the three orders and the one that looks most like a stone version of a wooden post.
The Eastern Roman Empire ran for a thousand years after Rome fell, with a court so layered in ceremony and intrigue that its name became the English word for anything needlessly complicated.

The Philistines were a real people with cities, pottery and trade. Matthew Arnold popularised the cultural insult in the 1860s, aiming it at the English middle classes — so an ancient nation is now a synonym for bad taste.
The oracle told Croesus that if he attacked Persia he would destroy a great empire. He attacked. The empire he destroyed was his own. Delphic answers were always true and almost never useful.
Philip of Macedon warned Sparta that if he entered Laconia he would raze it to the ground. The Spartans sent back a one-word reply: If. He did not invade.
Adam simply means man or earth in Hebrew — he is named after the ground he was made from. Adamic language means the supposed original speech of humanity, before Babel scattered it.

After the flood, the covenant with Noah is made with all humanity rather than one people, and the rainbow is its sign. Flood stories appear across Mesopotamian literature, including one a thousand years older.
Judaism, Christianity and Islam all trace themselves to Abraham, which is why they are grouped under his name. It is one of the few labels all three traditions accept.

Raised after four days in the tomb. The name is now used for anything that comes back when it should not: Lazarus taxa in biology are species that reappear in the fossil record long after apparently going extinct.
Prodigal means wastefully extravagant, not returning — the son is prodigal in the first half of the parable, before he comes home. People use it to mean the coming back, which is exactly backwards.

Mary Magdalene was identified with a penitent sinner by a pope in 591, on no textual basis, and the Church formally separated them again in 1969. Her name also gave English maudlin — from paintings of her weeping.

The Pharisees were a reform movement that made scripture accessible outside the Temple, and rabbinic Judaism descends from them. The English insult comes entirely from how the Gospels portray their arguments.

The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, and they rejected any belief in resurrection. When the Temple was destroyed in AD 70 they vanished with it, leaving the Pharisees to shape everything that came after.

Babylon really did have the scale the legends suggest — walls, ziggurats, and possibly gardens. Its reputation for decadence comes mostly from the people it conquered, who had every reason to be unkind.

mean: Confused mixture of voices or languages
story: The Babylonians called their city bab-ilu, gate of the god. Hebrew writers heard it as balal, to confuse, and built the story of the scattered languages around the pun. The tower was probably a real ziggurat.
One family name became the word for supreme ruler in half of Europe, and outlasted the empire by fifteen centuries. Caesar himself was never emperor — the title did not exist yet when he was killed.

German emperors were Kaisers right up to 1918, and the word is Caesar worn down by two thousand years of German mouths. The pronunciation is actually closer to the original Latin than the English Caesar is.

Given absolute power to save Rome, Cincinnatus won the war in about a fortnight, resigned, and went back to his farm. George Washington was compared to him constantly — and an American city is named for the society that admired him.

Pyrrho argued you should suspend judgement about everything, since certainty is not available. Sceptics after him used his name. He is not the Pyrrhus of the costly victory — two different Greeks, frequently confused.

Named after a painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught. The core claim is that you control your own judgements and nothing else — and two of its greatest writers were an enslaved man and a Roman emperor.

From the Greek for dog-like, meant as an insult about living rough in public. The Cynics accepted it. Their point was that convention is arbitrary; modern cynicism, assuming everyone is selfish, is a much later invention.

The Sophists were paid teachers of rhetoric in a city where winning an argument in court could save your life. Plato disliked them intensely, wrote the dialogues that survived, and their name has been an insult ever since.

Galen dissected pigs and apes because Roman law forbade human dissection, then described human anatomy from what he found. His errors went uncorrected for fourteen hundred years, because questioning Galen was unthinkable.
Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was the standard European medical textbook for six centuries — longer than it was used in the world that produced it. He wrote it in Persia around 1025.

Vesalius dissected human bodies himself rather than lecturing while an assistant did the cutting, and found more than two hundred places where Galen was wrong. He published at twenty-eight and was attacked for it immediately.

Harvey proved blood circulates by simple arithmetic: the heart pumps more blood in an hour than the whole body contains, so it cannot be constantly made and consumed. It must go round. His practice suffered for saying so.

Lister sprayed carbolic acid in operating theatres and death rates collapsed. Surgeons resented the implication that they carried infection on their own hands, and adoption took years longer than the evidence warranted.
The tremor Parkinson described is at its worst at rest and eases when the hand does something — the reverse of most tremors. That detail is still one of the first things a neurologist looks for.
The name is not Greek but Semitic — adon means lord, and the story travelled west from Phoenicia. So calling a handsome man an Adonis is a compliment in a language almost nobody using it knows.
From al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician of the ninth century. His name latinised to Algoritmi. Another of his book titles gave English a second word — al-jabr became algebra.

Ampere founded the study of electromagnetism in a few weeks of intense work after hearing that a current deflects a compass needle. His father had been guillotined during the Revolution when he was eighteen.

Louis Braille was blinded at three by an accident in his father's workshop. At fifteen he adapted a military code for reading messages in the dark into a six-dot alphabet. His school did not adopt it until after his death.
Celsius put 0 at boiling and 100 at freezing — the exact reverse of today's scale. It was flipped after he died, so the version everyone uses is upside down from the one he proposed.

mean: Excessive or fanatical patriotism; later broadened to prejudice (e.g., male chauvinism)
story: Nicolas Chauvin was supposedly a soldier so devoted to Napoleon that he stayed loyal after everyone else gave up. Historians have never found evidence he existed. The word may be named after a man who was never born.

Doppler predicted the effect using starlight in 1842. Three years later a Dutch scientist tested it by hiring a train, filling an open carriage with trumpeters, and posting musicians along the track to write down what they heard.

Fahrenheit set zero at the coldest temperature he could reliably reproduce — a mix of ice, water and salt. That is why the landmarks look arbitrary: they were pinned to what he could make in a bucket.

Galvani made a dead frog's leg twitch with electricity and concluded animals carry their own vital force. Volta disagreed, and invented the battery to prove it. Galvani was wrong, and English kept his name anyway.

McAdam worked out that a road needs no heavy stone foundation if it is raised, drained, and surfaced with small angular stones that lock together under traffic. Add tar to keep the dust down and you get tarmac.

Jean Martinet drilled Louis XIV's infantry into the best in Europe and was loathed for it. He was killed at the siege of Duisburg in 1672 by his own side's artillery, which some of his troops are said to have found fitting.

Mausolus ruled a small kingdom and his widow built him a tomb so vast it became one of the Seven Wonders. It stood for sixteen centuries, was destroyed by earthquakes, and its stone was carted off to build a castle.

Nemesis did not punish crime — she punished excess. Too much luck, too much boasting, and she arrived to restore the balance. Her name now means an unbeatable rival, which is a demotion from goddess of cosmic accounting.

Panacea and Hygieia were sisters, daughters of the god of medicine — one the cure for everything, the other the prevention. English kept both, and uses panacea almost entirely to say that no such thing exists.

The Earl of Sandwich asked for meat between bread so he could keep working — or keep gambling, depending on who is telling it. The gambling version comes from a political opponent, so it may be an insult that stuck.

Adolphe Sax survived falling from a third floor, swallowing a pin, drinking acid by mistake and a gunpowder explosion, all before adulthood. His mother said he was a child doomed to misfortune. He invented the saxophone at thirty.
Homer says the herald Stentor could shout as loudly as fifty men together. In one version he challenges a god to a shouting match, loses, and dies of it — which is a very specific way to go.
Sybaris was so wealthy that its citizens were said to have banned noisy trades from the city so nobody's sleep was disturbed. A rival city destroyed it in 510 BC and diverted a river over the ruins.

Tesla claimed to see detailed visions of his inventions before building them, and tested some purely in his head. He died in a New York hotel room, owing money, having given away most of the patents that made others rich.

Watt did not invent the steam engine — he made an existing one three times more efficient by adding a separate condenser. He also coined horsepower, as a sales device to explain his engines to people who owned horses.

Count Zeppelin was fifty-two and retired when he started building airships. The Hindenburg disaster ended the industry in thirty-seven seconds of newsreel — and a British rock band took the name a generation later.

mean: A smugly conventional businessman who prizes fitting in above all
story: Sinclair Lewis invented a realtor named George Babbitt who bought whatever his neighbours bought and believed whatever his club believed. Readers recognised him instantly — and within a year Americans were calling any such man a Babbitt.

Jeremy Bentham thought morality should be arithmetic — add up the happiness, subtract the suffering, keep whatever comes out positive. He left his body to University College London, where his preserved skeleton, dressed in his own clothes, still sits in a cabinet.

mean: A habit of imagining oneself as grander than one is
story: Emma Bovary read so many romances that her real life — a country doctor, a quiet village — became unbearable by comparison. The French coined bovarysme for that exact ache: mistaking the daydream for the life you were owed.

Swift sent Gulliver first to Lilliput, where he was a giant, then to Brobdingnag, where he was a toy. English kept both: lilliputian for the tiny, Brobdingnagian for the colossal. Only one of them is hard to spell.

mean: Resembling Bunyan's plain, vivid allegorical style
story: John Bunyan wrote The Pilgrim's Progress in Bedford jail, turning a Christian's life into a journey past the Slough of Despond and Vanity Fair. He had almost no schooling, and his plain thundering English outsold nearly every book in the language.

mean: An innocent optimist unshaken by disaster
story: Voltaire wrote Candide in three days to mock philosophers who insisted everything happens for the best. His hero endures catastrophe after catastrophe, and ends up concluding only this: we must cultivate our garden.

mean: Someone whose accurate warnings are ignored
story: Cassandra saw Troy burn years before it happened. She warned everyone. Apollo's curse meant her family heard her perfectly and dismissed her every time — the cruellest gift in Greek myth, and now the word for any warning nobody heeds.

mean: Bewitching in a way that degrades
story: Circe welcomed Odysseus's sailors with wine and cheese, then touched them with her wand and watched them drop to all fours as swine. Odysseus, protected by a herb from Hermes, was the one guest she could not transform.

mean: Eloquent and polished in the classical manner
story: Cicero could hold the Roman Senate for hours with sentences built like architecture. Renaissance scholars admired him so much that some refused to use any Latin word he had not used first — a fussiness their rivals mocked as Ciceronian.

Exiled from Florence on pain of burning, Dante spent his banishment writing a tour of the afterlife — and quietly placed several of his political enemies in hell. A Dantesque scene is one of infernal, orderly horror.

Demosthenes is said to have practised with pebbles in his mouth and shouted over the surf to strengthen his voice. He turned that hard-won delivery on Philip of Macedon in speeches so fierce that attacks on any leader are still called philippics.

Nietzsche split art in two: Apollonian for order and clarity, Dionysian for ecstasy and abandon. Both named for gods — Apollo the composed archer, Dionysus the god whose worshippers danced themselves out of their own minds.

Euhemerus claimed to have found an inscription on a distant island proving Zeus had been an ordinary king. Nobody has ever located the island, but the idea stuck: euhemerism is the theory that every god started out as somebody's grandfather.

Falstaff lies about his own bravery so extravagantly that his friends count the exaggerations for sport. Legend says Queen Elizabeth enjoyed him so much she asked Shakespeare for a play showing the fat knight in love.

mean: Sacrificing what matters most for present gain
story: The real Johann Faust was a wandering German magician. Legend gave him a contract with the devil, Marlowe and Goethe gave him great plays, and English gained the Faustian bargain — a deal that pays now and ruins you later.

mean: A person of flawless nobility and purity
story: Every knight at the Round Table went looking for the Grail. Only Galahad, so pure he could sit in the one chair that killed all other occupants, was permitted to find it — and having found it, he was taken straight to heaven.

mean: Intricate; solved only by bold, direct action
story: For centuries nobody untied the Gordian knot. Alexander the Great arrived, considered it briefly, and cut it in half with his sword. He went on to conquer Asia, which suggests the oracle accepted his method.

Hamlet has the proof, the motive, and the opportunity by act three — and still stops to ask whether being is better than not being. Shakespeare made indecision so gripping that the prince's name became the word for it.

mean: A greedy snatcher; a persistent tormentor
story: The Harpies were storm spirits with women's faces and birds' bodies, sent to snatch the food from Phineus's table again and again. Their name comes from the Greek for 'snatchers', and it is still what we call anything that will not stop grabbing.

This one is unfair to Hector. In the Iliad he is the most decent man in the war — a devoted father defending his city. Later English writers recast him as a swaggerer, and to hector has meant to bully ever since.

Herostratus torched one of the Seven Wonders of the World and freely confessed his motive: fame. Ephesus made it a capital crime to speak his name, hoping to erase him. You are reading it now, which tells you how well that worked.

Conan Doyle based Holmes on his medical teacher Joseph Bell, who could diagnose a patient's trade and travels before they spoke. Doyle killed Holmes off at a waterfall; public outrage was so fierce he had to bring him back.

mean: Something of surpassing brightness or grandeur
story: Hyperion fathered Helios the sun, Selene the moon, and Eos the dawn. Hamlet uses him as the measure of magnificence — comparing his noble father to Hyperion and his uncle to a satyr. The tallest living tree on Earth carries the name.

Daedalus warned his son twice: not too low, or the sea will soak the feathers; not too high, or the sun will melt the wax. Icarus flew high anyway. The stretch of water where he fell is still called the Icarian Sea.

mean: A traitor, especially one who betrays a friend
story: Judas gave up his teacher for thirty silver coins and marked him with a kiss so the soldiers would know which man to take. Two thousand years later the name is still a synonym for betrayal, and almost nobody names a child Judas.

mean: A person with two violently opposed personalities
story: Stevenson is said to have written the first draft in three days, burned it after his wife's criticism, and rewritten the whole thing in three more. The result gave English its standard phrase for anyone who is two different people.

Jezebel painted her face and dressed her hair before meeting the men who came to overthrow her — defiant to the last minute. The Bible meant it as a portrait of vanity; her name has been an insult in English for four hundred years.

Kafka wrote about a man arrested for a crime the court refuses to name, and a surveyor who can never reach the castle that employs him. He asked his friend to burn all of it after his death. His friend published everything instead.

mean: Aged, raging, and betrayed by one's own family
story: Lear asks his three daughters to say how much they love him. Two lay it on thick; Cordelia, who means it, refuses to perform. He gives his kingdom to the flatterers and spends the rest of the play discovering his mistake in a storm.

Asked why he had ordered a magnificent dinner when he was eating alone, Lucullus is said to have replied that tonight Lucullus dines with Lucullus. He also brought the cherry tree to Italy, which may be his more useful legacy.

Machiavelli wrote The Prince while out of a job, partly hoping to be hired again. Within decades English playwrights had turned his name into a stock villain — the Machiavel — who smiles at you while planning exactly how to use you.

mean: A comic mix-up of similar-sounding words
story: Sheridan named her from the French mal a propos, 'badly suited'. She meant to call a man the pinnacle of politeness and called him the pineapple instead — and every mixed-up word since has carried her name.

mean: Lacking a wise guide or adviser
story: When Odysseus sailed for Troy he left his son in the care of a friend named Mentor. The goddess Athena kept borrowing that shape to deliver advice — so the word for a trusted guide is really the name of a disguise.

Merlin appears first in a twelfth-century history that presented him as fact. He is said to have aged backwards, remembering the future and forgetting the past — which is one way to explain a prophet who always knows what happens next.

mean: Grand, sublime, and epic in style
story: Milton went completely blind in his forties and composed Paradise Lost in his head at night, dictating each morning to whoever was available — often his daughters. Twelve books of epic poetry, and he never saw a line of it written down.

mean: Excessive attachment to or idealisation of mothers
story: Philip Wylie coined momism in Generation of Vipers, a book so scathing that it made him famous and disliked in equal measure. It is one of the rare eponyms built not from a person's name but from what a whole country called its mothers.

Morpheus did not bring sleep; he supplied the people in your dreams, taking their shapes himself. When a chemist isolated a powerful sleep-bringing drug from opium in 1804 he named it morphine after the same god.

mean: Marked by long wandering and clever survival
story: Odysseus escaped a cyclops by telling it his name was Nobody, so that its cries for help made no sense to the neighbours. Ten years of that kind of thinking got him home, and gave English both odyssey and Odyssean.

mean: Faithfully patient; also endlessly repeated work
story: Penelope told a hall full of suitors she would remarry once she finished weaving a shroud. Each night she quietly unravelled the day's work. She held them off for three years before a servant gave her away.

mean: Cheerfully naive; or of a word used in an odd, harmless sense
story: The Pickwick Papers made the twenty-four-year-old Dickens famous in monthly instalments. It also gave English a strange, useful phrase: to mean something in a Pickwickian sense is to insist your insult does not count.

Proteus knew everything but hated being asked. Grab him and he becomes a lion, then a snake, then running water, then a tree — and only when you have held on through all of it does he give up and tell you the truth.

mean: Boisterously earthy and exuberant in humour
story: Rabelais wrote about giants so large that a whole army once sheltered under one's tongue. His books were banned by the theologians of the Sorbonne, which did nothing to slow their sales and gave French a word for cheerful excess.

Two women each swore the baby was hers. Solomon called for a sword and offered to give each of them half. One agreed; the other begged him to give the child away instead — and he handed the baby to her.

Shylock's bond entitles him to a pound of flesh, and the court agrees it is valid — then rules he may take flesh but not one drop of blood, because the contract never mentioned blood. He loses on the same literal reading he demanded.

Thomas More described a perfect island republic and named it, in Greek, No Place. Everyone since has used utopia to mean a paradise, missing the pun. More was beheaded by Henry VIII, which was not utopian at all.

mean: Producing electric current by chemical action
story: Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with brine-soaked cloth between them and made electricity flow steadily for the first time. Napoleon made him a count. The volt is named for him too, so he is one of very few people who are twice a unit.

Alcibiades led Athens, defected to Sparta, advised Persia, then came home to cheering crowds. Socrates taught him and could not steady him. He is the ancient world's model for the dazzling person you should probably not trust.

Creon forbade the burial of Antigone's brother on pain of death. She scattered earth over his body anyway and told the king to his face that no decree of his could overrule the unwritten laws. She was walled up alive for it.

Hermes eventually bored Argus to sleep with stories and killed him. Hera gathered his hundred eyes and set them into the tail of her peacock, which is why the bird still looks like it is watching you from every direction.

Rome so distrusted the Bacchanalia that the Senate banned them in 186 BC and executed thousands of participants. The god survived the crackdown, and English kept bacchic and bacchanal for any party that goes well past sensible.

Belisarius reconquered North Africa and Italy for an emperor who never quite trusted him, and was twice stripped of command. A later legend, probably false, had him blinded and begging in the streets — a story too good for painters to resist.

mean: Of a message that harms the person carrying it
story: Bellerophon delivered his own death warrant, unaware, because he could not read the sealed tablet he carried. The king who received it sent him to fight the Chimera instead — and he survived that too, on the back of the winged horse Pegasus.

Zeus was losing the war against the Titans until he freed three hundred-handed giants from the underworld. Briareus and his brothers hurled three hundred boulders at once, and the Titans broke. Some jobs need more hands than others.

mean: Favouring tradition and cautious, gradual change
story: Burke supported the American colonists and opposed the French revolutionaries, which sounds inconsistent until you notice his rule: mend what exists, do not tear it down and start fresh. His prediction that France would end under a general came true.

Caesar's name outlived his empire twice over: German emperors were Kaisers and Russian ones Tsars, both worn-down forms of Caesar. The surgical caesarean also carries it, though the old story that he was born that way is almost certainly untrue.

Caligula was a soldiers' nickname meaning 'little boot' — he wore a miniature army uniform as a child on campaign with his father. The cuddly nickname stuck to one of the most feared names in Roman history.

mean: Alluringly detaining; keeping someone from leaving
story: Calypso offered Odysseus eternal youth and a beautiful island forever. He sat on the shore and wept because he wanted to go home to a middle-aged wife on a rocky one. The gods eventually made her let him go.

Whatever the Senate was debating — roads, taxes, anything — Cato finished his speech with the same line: and furthermore, Carthage must be destroyed. He kept it up for years. Eventually Rome destroyed Carthage.

Cerberus had three heads so at least one was always awake. The trick was music — Orpheus played him to sleep — or cake, since the Romans buried honey cakes with the dead specifically as a bribe. Hence a sop to Cerberus.

Odysseus had to steer between Scylla's six heads and Charybdis's whirlpool. Choosing Scylla cost him six men; Charybdis would have cost the ship. Between Scylla and Charybdis still means a choice between two disasters.

Agamemnon sacrificed their daughter to get his fleet to Troy. Clytemnestra waited ten years, welcomed him home across a purple carpet, and killed him in his bath. Greek tragedy rarely takes a clear side on which of them was worse.

Croesus asked an oracle whether to attack Persia and was told he would destroy a great empire. He attacked. The empire he destroyed was his own. Rich as Croesus survived him by two and a half thousand years.

Daedalus designed the Labyrinth so cunningly that he could barely find his own way out of it. King Minos imprisoned him to keep the secret, so he built wings. His son Icarus did not follow the flight instructions.

Diomedes is the only mortal in the Iliad to wound two gods in one afternoon. Athena lends him the sight to tell gods from men on the battlefield, and he uses it immediately to pick a fight with the god of war.

Erasmus produced the Greek New Testament that Luther translated from, then spent the Reformation refusing to join either side. Both sides attacked him. He said he would rather be a spectator than a soldier in a war of words.

mean: Adherence to Euclid's geometry or axiomatic method
story: Euclid's Elements was a school textbook for over two thousand years — the longest run of any book but the Bible. Asked by a king for a shortcut, he is supposed to have replied that there is no royal road to geometry.

mean: Achieving results by patient delay rather than direct attack
story: Rome nicknamed Fabius the Delayer as an insult; after Hannibal destroyed a Roman army that did attack, it became a compliment. Britain's Fabian Society took the name in 1884 to signal socialism by patience rather than revolution.

mean: Of Florence; in cooking, served with spinach
story: Catherine de' Medici left Florence in 1533 to marry the future king of France, reportedly bringing her own cooks and a fondness for spinach. Whether or not the story is true, French menus have called spinach dishes a la florentine ever since.

mean: Relating to Galileo's discoveries or relativity
story: In January 1610 Galileo pointed a homemade telescope at Jupiter and saw three little stars beside it. Four nights later they had moved. They were moons, orbiting something other than Earth — and the sky was never the same shape again.

mean: Of an idealised creation brought to life
story: Pygmalion carved a woman more perfect than any living one and then could not stop loving her. Aphrodite took pity and warmed the ivory to skin. Shaw reused the plot in Pygmalion, which became My Fair Lady.

mean: To petrify or paralyse with a stare
story: There were three Gorgons, but only Medusa could be killed. Perseus managed it by never looking at her directly — he watched her reflection in his polished shield and struck at what he saw there.

mean: A wood nymph; also the king cobra
story: A dryad could wander the forest. A hamadryad could not: she lived inside a single tree and her life ended with it, so cutting one down was murder. Naturalists later borrowed the name for the king cobra.

Roman satire came in two flavours: Horatian, which laughs at you, and Juvenalian, which wants you punished. Horace also gave us carpe diem — seize the day — from a poem about opening the wine now rather than later.

Eirene was one of three sisters who kept the seasons and the social order. Athens raised a statue of her holding the infant god of wealth, making the point plainly: peace is what makes prosperity possible.

Greek poets rarely said Thebes when they could say something more ornate. Ismenean, after the river running past the city, was the elegant option — the kind of word that tells you the writer had a classical education.

mean: Majestic and genial; or relating to Jupiter
story: Jove gave English two words with opposite moods. Jovial means cheerful, because Jupiter's influence was thought lucky. Saturnine means gloomy, from Saturn. Your temperament, medieval doctors believed, depended on which planet was up when you were born.

Lucian wrote A True Story, about sailing to the moon and meeting its army — and opened by announcing that everything in it was a lie. Scholars call it the first science fiction, written eighteen centuries before the rockets.

mean: Severely disciplined in law and custom
story: Lycurgus supposedly made the Spartans swear to keep his laws until he returned, then left and never came back — binding them forever by a technicality. Whether he existed at all is still argued over.

Perseus cut off Medusa's head and the winged horse Pegasus sprang from her neck. He kept the head as a weapon — it worked just as well detached — and eventually gave it to Athena, who mounted it on her shield.

Minerva was born from her father's skull, fully grown and already in armour, after he swallowed her mother. The owl on her shoulder is why owls have stood for wisdom in Western art for two thousand years.

mean: A follower who obeys orders unquestioningly
story: Myrmex is Greek for ant. When a plague emptied the island of Aegina, Zeus turned its ants into people — and they kept the ant temperament: tireless, obedient, and utterly without independent opinions.

Nereus had fifty daughters and they were the good sort of sea spirit — they helped sailors rather than drowning them. Neptune's second-largest moon is called Nereid, and so is a whole class of bristly marine worms.

Niobe said she was luckier than a goddess who had only two children. Apollo and Artemis — the two children in question — killed all fourteen of hers. She wept until she became a rock, and the rock kept weeping.

Orpheus played so beautifully that Hades agreed to release Eurydice — on one condition: do not look back until you are both in daylight. He was almost out when he turned around to check she was following.

mean: Of vanished power and grandiose ruin
story: Shelley wrote the sonnet as a bet with a friend over who could write the better poem about Egypt. The inscription in it — look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair — sits on a broken statue in an empty desert.

Pericles spent the treasury of an alliance on rebuilding his own city, which the allies noticed. The Parthenon was the result. He died of plague three years into the war that ended the age named after him.

mean: Of Phoenicia; relating to its traders and alphabet
story: The Phoenicians were merchants, not conquerors, and their greatest export was not cloth or cedar but the alphabet. Every letter you are reading descends from marks made by traders who needed a quick way to keep accounts.

Poe's raven comes from the Night's Plutonian shore. When an eleven-year-old girl suggested Pluto for the new planet in 1930, the underworld god fit — it was the coldest, darkest, farthest thing anyone had found.

mean: Boldly original and defiant of limits
story: Zeus chained Prometheus to a mountain and sent an eagle to eat his liver each day; it grew back each night. Mary Shelley subtitled Frankenstein 'The Modern Prometheus' — a warning about the cost of stealing fire.

Sappho was so admired that Plato called her the tenth Muse, yet almost all of her nine books are lost — we have one complete poem and a drift of fragments, some recovered from ancient rubbish dumps in Egypt.
Medieval doctors believed the planet overhead at your birth set your personality for life. Saturn, slow and cold and distant, produced the melancholy sort. The planet has moved on; the word has not.

mean: Heroically resolving a seemingly impossible problem
story: Athens had been sending fourteen young people into the Labyrinth every nine years as tribute. Theseus volunteered to be one of them, killed the monster at the centre, and ended the tribute — which is how you get a city named after you.

Thebes was where Greek tragedy went for its worst stories: a king who married his mother, a daughter buried alive, brothers who killed each other at the gates. Alexander the Great later flattened the city, sparing only the poet Pindar's house.

mean: Produced or carried by the wind
