story: Aeolus bagged up the contrary winds so Odysseus could sail straight home. In sight of Ithaca the crew opened the bag, assuming it held treasure, and blew themselves all the way back. Geologists still call wind-blown sand aeolian.

mean: Of a commanding leader met with a terrible end
story: Agamemnon won the ten-year war and survived the whole of it, only to be killed in his own bathroom within hours of arriving home. Schliemann dug up a gold funeral mask at Mycenae and cabled that he had gazed on the face of Agamemnon. It was three centuries too old.

mean: A figure of great strength brought down by wounded pride
story: Ajax was the wall of the Greek army — the man who never lost a duel. He killed himself over a prize he did not win. A cleaning powder now carries his name, on the reasoning that it is stronger than dirt.

mean: Of Andromeda; of the neighbouring galaxy
story: Andromeda's mother said her daughter was lovelier than the sea nymphs, and a monster was sent to collect the difference. Perseus saved her mid-flight. The whole family — mother, father, hero, monster — was put in the sky as constellations.

mean: Having enormous strength drawn from the ground
story: Antaeus beat every wrestler who came at him, because every time he was thrown down he got up stronger. Heracles worked out the trick, hoisted him off the ground, and held him in the air until he weakened.

Nietzsche paired Apollonian order against Dionysian ecstasy and argued great art needs both — the clear shape and the wild energy inside it. The Apollo space programme took the name of the god who drove the sun across the sky.

Arachne's tapestry was better than the goddess's — that was the problem. Athena tore it up and struck her, and when Arachne despaired, turned her into a creature that could weave forever. Spiders are still classed as arachnids.

The Areopagus tried murder cases, and myth says its first defendant was the war god Ares himself. Milton borrowed the name in 1644 for Areopagitica, his argument against censorship — a speech to a court that no longer existed.

mean: An adventurer on a difficult quest
story: The Argonauts were named for their ship, not their leader — argonaut simply means Argo-sailor. Prospectors racing to California in 1849 called themselves Argonauts too, which was optimistic about the fleece.

Aristophanes wrote a comedy attacking Socrates as a fraud who taught students to dodge debts. Twenty-four years later, at his trial, Socrates complained that the play had poisoned the jury against him long before he arrived.

Aristotle tutored Alexander the Great, dissected sea creatures on Lesbos, and wrote the first surviving works on logic, physics and drama. For much of the Middle Ages, European scholars simply called him The Philosopher.

The Roman Senate banned the Bacchanalia in 186 BC, calling them a conspiracy. Thousands were arrested. The festivals had grown from a small women's rite into all-night gatherings the state could neither see into nor control.

mean: Betraying a friend out of principle
story: Shakespeare gives the dying Caesar the line Et tu, Brute — you too, Brutus. The real Caesar probably said nothing at all. Brutus insisted he acted for the Republic, not against the man, and killed himself two years later.

mean: Of a victory that ruins the victor
story: A Cadmean victory costs more than losing would have. Cadmus also, according to the Greeks, brought them the alphabet from Phoenicia — so the man behind the ruinous win is also the reason they could write about it.

mean: Grandly epic; also loud and brassy
story: Calliope was the eldest Muse and the mother of Orpheus. In 1855 an American inventor attached her name to a steam whistle organ so loud it could be heard for miles — the calliope that still shrieks over fairgrounds.

mean: A sculpted female figure used as a pillar
story: Six caryatids hold up a porch of the Erechtheion in Athens. One was removed by Lord Elgin and taken to London; the Athenians said for years that the remaining five could be heard at night, crying for their missing sister.

The Greeks buried their dead with a coin in the mouth to pay Charon. Anyone unburied waited a hundred years on the wrong bank. Pluto's largest moon is named Charon, still ferrying alongside the underworld.

Clio's name comes from the Greek for 'to make famous' — the historian's actual job, as the Greeks saw it. Herodotus's nine books of history were each named after one of the nine Muses, and Clio got book one.

Three sisters ran every life: Clotho spun the thread, Lachesis measured it, Atropos cut. Even Zeus could not overrule them. Engineers borrowed the name for the clothoid, the spiralling curve that eases a road into a bend.

mean: Of Saturn; belonging to a remote golden age
story: Cronus swallowed each of his children at birth to stop the prophecy that one would overthrow him. His wife handed him a stone in swaddling clothes instead of the sixth. The sixth was Zeus, and the prophecy held.

For nearly two thousand years, thousands of Greeks were initiated at Eleusis — and not one of them ever recorded what happened inside. The penalty for telling was death. It remains the best-kept secret in the ancient world.
Elysium was the good afterlife — sunlight, meadows, no work. Paris named a boulevard after it: the Champs-Elysees, the Elysian Fields. Anyone stuck in its traffic may question the comparison.

The Furies hunted murderers without rest. Calling them the Eumenides — the Kindly Ones — was pure superstition: you did not want to attract their attention by using the real name. It is the oldest recorded nickname made out of fear.

mean: Of something lost at the final moment by looking back
story: One rule: do not look back until you are both out. Orpheus walked the whole way up in silence, heard nothing behind him, and turned at the last step to check. She was there, and then she was not.

mean: Of the Hebrew language, people or tradition
story: Hebrew stopped being an everyday spoken language for roughly seventeen centuries, surviving only in prayer and study — then was deliberately revived, and is now the first language of millions. No other language has managed that.

mean: Witchlike; of the night and crossroads
story: Hecate is often shown with three faces, watching all three roads at once. Greeks left food for her at junctions on the night of the new moon, and did not look too closely at who collected it.

mean: Of a beauty that causes conflict
story: Careful with the spelling: Helenic is Helen of Troy, Hellenic is Greek in general. Both trace to Greece, but only one of them started a ten-year war by leaving with a visiting prince.

Hephaestus was thrown off Olympus as an infant and walked with difficulty afterwards — the only Greek god with a disability. He was also the only one who actually made things, including golden servants that moved on their own.

mean: Of a deep purple-blue; of thick curling hair
story: Apollo threw the discus, the wind blew it off course, and his friend died. The flower that grew where the blood fell carried the boy's name. Homer uses hyacinthine for hair, meaning dark and tightly curled.

mean: Epic in the scale of its conflict
story: The Iliad is not about the whole war — it covers about seven weeks near the end, and never reaches the wooden horse. Its actual subject, announced in the first word, is the anger of one man.

mean: Of one sacrificed for a larger cause
story: Agamemnon summoned his daughter to the coast on the pretext of a wedding. In some versions Artemis snatched her away at the last instant and left a deer on the altar — a rescue the Greeks invented later, when the original proved unbearable.

The dead drank from Lethe so they could start again with nothing. Its opposite, Mnemosyne, ran alongside — and initiates of some mystery cults were told to refuse the first river and ask for the second.

The Lycians cut house-shaped tombs high into sheer rock so the dead would be closer to the sky. Their alphabet borrowed from Greek but kept extra letters for sounds Greek did not have, and nobody could read it for two thousand years.

Medea gave up her home and her family to help Jason steal the Golden Fleece. When he left her for a princess, she destroyed everything he loved and escaped in a chariot drawn by dragons. Euripides gave her the last word.

Melpomene started as the Muse of singing — her name means 'to celebrate with song'. She was reassigned to tragedy later. The two masks hanging outside theatres are hers and her sister Thalia's, comedy and tragedy together.

The Greeks made memory the mother of the arts, which is exactly right for a culture that recited Homer from memory for centuries before writing it down. Mnemonic — a memory trick — comes from the same root.

Nemesis did not punish crime — she punished excess. Too much luck, too much boasting, and she arrived to restore the balance. Her name now means an unbeatable rival, which is a demotion from goddess of cosmic accounting.
For the earliest Greeks the Ocean was not water everywhere — it was one enormous river running in a circle around the rim of a flat world, and Oceanus was the Titan who was that river.

mean: A four-year period; the Olympic Games
story: An Olympiad is properly the four-year gap, not the festival — the Greeks dated events by counting them. The ancient games ran for roughly twelve centuries before a Roman emperor shut them down as a pagan rite.

Perseus borrowed winged sandals, a cap of invisibility and a mirrored shield, which is a lot of equipment for one monster. The Perseid meteor shower every August appears to come from his constellation.

mean: Of the nightingale; of song born from sorrow
story: Philomela was silenced and wove her story into a tapestry instead, because nobody thought to take away her loom. The gods turned her into a nightingale — the bird that sings most beautifully after dark.

Rhadamanthus was one of three judges deciding where each soul went, and he had the reputation of being unbribable. His name is now the strongest word English has for a judge who will not bend, not even slightly.

Selene fell in love with a shepherd and asked Zeus to keep him young forever; he granted it by putting the man into eternal sleep. The element selenium is named after her, because it was found alongside one named for the earth.

Terpsichore is the reason a dancer can be called a terpsichorean — a nine-letter way of saying it. Of the nine Muses she is the one whose job survives most recognisably: she is usually shown mid-step, holding a lyre.

Romans thought the rumble of Etna was Vulcan hammering underground. The island of Vulcano off Sicily was his chimney, and it gave every volcano on Earth its name — including the ones nowhere near Italy.

A small Roman town called Hadria named the whole Adriatic Sea, then lent its adjective to the emperor Hadrian, then to popes and a great many children. The town itself is now several miles inland, left behind by the silt.

Virgil's stock epithet for him is pius Aeneas — not pious exactly, but dutiful. He escapes Troy with his father on his back and his household gods under his arm, and spends the rest of the poem doing what he is told by fate.

Greek had at least four words for love, and early Christian writers deliberately picked the least romantic one. Agape is not affection or desire — it is the kind you extend to someone who has done nothing to earn it.

Admetus was allowed to escape death if someone would go instead. He asked his parents, who declined. His wife Alcestis volunteered. Heracles turned up, heard the story, and went to wrestle Death at the graveside to get her back.

Zeus disguised himself as Amphitryon to visit his wife, producing two identical husbands and a very confused household. Moliere's version settles the question with a line the French adopted: the real Amphitryon is the one who serves the meal.
The image of Aeneas escaping Troy with his father on his back and his son by the hand became Rome's picture of duty itself — carrying the past out and leading the future forward at the same time.

A London gentlemen's club sang a drinking song called To Anacreon in Heaven. An American lawyer later set his poem about a flag to that same tune, and the United States ended up with a national anthem built on a Greek wine poet.
Anchorites went further than monks: some were sealed into a small cell attached to a church wall, with one window to the altar and one to the street, and stayed there for the rest of their lives.

mean: Of a classical golden age in literature
story: Augustus boasted he found Rome brick and left it marble. Eighteenth-century English writers admired the period so much that they called their own era Augustan and set out to imitate it deliberately.
This is an ancient insult that outlived its target. Athens sneered at Boeotia as farmland full of dullards — conveniently forgetting that Hesiod, Pindar and Plutarch all came from there.

mean: Comically idealistic in the manner of Cervantes
story: Cervantes lost the use of his left hand at the battle of Lepanto and spent five years as a captive in Algiers before writing what is often called the first modern novel. He died in the same week as Shakespeare.

mean: Of the Americas or of Columbus
story: America was named for Amerigo Vespucci, not Columbus — but Columbian survived as the poetic alternative. It is why the United States has a District of Columbia and Canada a British Columbia.

Coriolanus could not bring himself to show his battle scars to voters, which was the custom. Exiled for the insult, he marched on Rome and was stopped only when his mother walked out to meet the army.

Cressida does not appear in Homer at all — she was invented in the Middle Ages and handed down through Boccaccio and Chaucer to Shakespeare, each of whom made her a little less sympathetic than the last.

mean: Eloquently romantic while hidden behind another
story: The real Cyrano wrote science fiction about travelling to the moon. Rostand gave him an enormous nose, a duelling sword, and the finest words in French theatre — all spent under a balcony, for another man.
Dante wrote the Divine Comedy in Italian rather than Latin, which scholars considered a waste of a good poem. It is the reason modern Italian sounds the way it does.

Diogenes walked Athens in daylight with a lit lamp, saying he was looking for an honest man. When Alexander the Great offered him anything he wanted, he asked him to move slightly — he was blocking the sun.

Don Quixote's windmills are the most famous mistake in literature. Cervantes meant to mock outdated romances, but readers kept siding with the old man who insisted the world should be nobler than it is.

mean: Of the Dorians; of the Doric style or mode
story: The Doric column is the plain one — no scrolls, no leaves, just fluting and a flat top. Greeks thought of it as the masculine, unfussy order, and used it for the Parthenon.

mean: Of Euclid's geometry, in which parallel lines never meet
story: Euclid's fifth postulate — about parallel lines — bothered mathematicians for centuries because it seemed like it should be provable. It is not. Dropping it produced curved, non-Euclidean geometries, and eventually general relativity.

mean: Of the Gospel; zealously spreading a message
story: Euangelion literally means good message — in classical Greek it was the reward you gave the runner who brought good news from a battle. English kept the messenger sense in evangelist and the enthusiasm in evangelical.

mean: Of the modern calendar or of plainsong chant
story: To fix the drift, October 1582 simply lost ten days — people went to sleep on the 4th and woke on the 15th. Britain held out until 1752, by which time it had to skip eleven.
Swift wrote Gulliver's Travels as savage political satire. It was so successful as an adventure story that it turned into a children's book, which is the fate of a surprising number of angry books.

mean: Of an apparent choice that is really no choice
story: Hobson had forty horses and a rule that stopped customers from wearing out the best ones. Students grumbled about Hobson's choice, and the phrase outlived every horse in the stable.

Johnson spent nine years on his dictionary and slipped jokes into it — he defined lexicographer as a harmless drudge. His friend Boswell wrote down his conversation for years, producing the most famous biography in English.

mean: Of Kant's philosophy of reason and duty
story: Kant kept to a schedule so exact that neighbours in Konigsberg were said to set their clocks by his afternoon walk. He never travelled more than a hundred miles from his birthplace, and rearranged Western philosophy from there.

Lilliput's great political dispute is whether to crack a boiled egg at the big end or the little end — a war that has killed thousands. Swift was writing about religious conflict, and he was not being subtle.

Lucifer is Latin for light-bringer and was originally the morning star, Venus. A verse in Isaiah about a fallen Babylonian king was read as being about Satan, and the planet's name transferred to the devil.

Newton did his best work during a plague year when Cambridge closed and he went home to the farm. In eighteen months he laid out calculus, optics and gravitation. He later called it his year of wonders.

mean: Of the Petrarchan sonnet; of idealised unattainable love
story: Petrarch saw Laura in a church in Avignon in 1327 and wrote poems about her for the next forty years, including twenty-one after her death. There is no evidence they ever had a conversation.

Defoe based Crusoe partly on Alexander Selkirk, a Scottish sailor marooned for four years on a Pacific island. Germans coined Robinsonade for the flood of imitations, and the genre now includes Swiss Family Robinson and Lord of the Flies.

mean: Of Victoria's reign; strait-laced and formal
story: Victoria came to the throne at eighteen and reigned longer than any British monarch before her. The word Victorian now suggests prudishness, though the queen herself wrote frankly in her diaries about how much she adored her husband.

mean: Given to constant or foolish laughter
story: Abdera produced Democritus, who worked out that matter is made of atoms twenty-three centuries early, and who reportedly could not stop laughing at people. The town's neighbours took the laughter personally.
Deported Acadians who reached Louisiana were called Acadiens, then Cadiens, then Cajuns. The whole of Cajun food, music and dialect traces back to one forced expulsion from the far north.

mean: Strikingly handsome; also a short verse line
story: The name is not Greek but Semitic — adon means lord, and the story came west from Phoenicia. Calling a handsome man an Adonis is therefore a compliment in a language most people using it do not know.

mean: Being produced or shaped by wind
story: An aeolian harp is left in an open window and plays itself. Romantic poets loved the idea — an instrument with no performer — and used it as an image for inspiration arriving from somewhere outside you.

mean: Conveying meaning indirectly, to evade censors
story: Aesop was said to be an enslaved man who won his freedom through cleverness. In Soviet Russia, Aesopian language meant writing your real point in code — because the fable was still the safest way to criticise power.
Alcinous had a garden where fruit ripened all year round and never failed. He also had the good manners to feed his exhausted guest for two days before asking him who he was.

Alcuin's scribes developed a clear rounded script called Carolingian minuscule to replace the tangle scribes had been using. Renaissance printers copied it, and the lower-case letters you are reading now descend directly from it.
Amalthea's broken horn became the cornucopia — the horn of plenty still drawn overflowing with fruit at harvest festivals. Zeus later set her among the stars in gratitude for the milk.

Camel caravans camped at the temple of Amun, and a white salt crusted the ground where they did. Romans called it sal ammoniac, salt of Amun. Every bottle of ammonia is named after an Egyptian god by way of camel dung.

mean: Of the peak of the Roman Empire
story: The Antonine Wall was built across Scotland under him, north of Hadrian's, and abandoned within about twenty years. Rome kept the older wall — the one named after the emperor who did less building.

The recipes attributed to Apicius include flamingo and dormice stuffed with pork. Legend says he poisoned himself on discovering he had only a modest fortune left and could no longer eat as he wished.

mean: Experimentally modern in the manner of Apollinaire
story: Apollinaire wrote calligrammes — poems typeset in the shape of a horse, the Eiffel Tower, falling rain. He also invented the word surrealism, three years before the movement that took it existed.

Aristarchus went through Homer marking every line he thought was a later addition, using a small horizontal stroke in the margin. That stroke is the ancestor of the obelus, and the dagger symbol still used in footnotes.

mean: Of Arnold's view of culture as moral improvement
story: Arnold spent his working life as a school inspector, travelling England examining classrooms, and wrote criticism in the gaps. He argued that culture was the antidote to what he called anarchy, by which he mostly meant the middle classes.
Athena and Poseidon competed for the city. He struck the rock and produced a salt spring; she planted an olive tree. The citizens chose the olive, and the city took her name.

mean: Elegantly simple; also a top storey
story: Attic salt means dry Athenian wit. The attic in your house is the same word: architects called a small decorative upper storey in the Athenian manner an attic storey, and the name slid up into the roof space.

mean: Illusory; generous in appearance but giving nothing
story: The Barmecide describes each imaginary course in loving detail while the beggar mimes eating it. The beggar plays along, then pretends to be drunk on imaginary wine and punches him — at which the prince laughs and serves a real dinner.

mean: Of an idealised woman as spiritual guide
story: Dante met Beatrice when they were both about nine and spoke to her only a handful of times. She married someone else and died at twenty-four. He put her in charge of heaven.

Bentham also designed the panopticon, a prison where one unseen guard could watch every cell. It was never built to his plan, but the idea has been borrowed by everyone writing about surveillance since.

Boethius wrote his masterpiece in a cell while waiting to be executed for treason. The wheel of fortune he described — lifting people up only to drop them — became the standard medieval image for how luck works.

mean: Crowded, earthy and full of incident
story: Bruegel painted a hundred children's games in a single picture and a village wedding where you can count the pies. In his Icarus, the boy falls out of the sky and every farmer in the painting keeps working.

mean: Of Brown's theory of medical excitability
story: Brown reduced medicine to one dial: too stimulated or not stimulated enough. Treatment was opium or alcohol accordingly. It was wrong, wildly popular across Europe, and probably killed more patients than it saved.

mean: Of Charlemagne's dynasty and its revival of learning
story: Charlemagne ruled most of western Europe and worked at learning to write late in life, keeping a tablet under his pillow to practise. He never quite managed it, but he made sure his empire's scribes could.
Apollo gave Cassandra prophecy hoping to win her affection. When she refused him he could not take the gift back, so he added a condition: she would always be right, and nobody would ever act on it.

mean: Intensely personal and direct in lyric
story: Catullus survives by luck — a single manuscript turned up in Verona around 1300 and vanished again after being copied. His most famous poem is two lines long and begins by saying he hates and loves at the same time.

Chaldean astronomers kept night-sky records for centuries and could predict eclipses. Greeks and Romans used Chaldean to mean fortune-teller, which was rather like calling an astronomer a horoscope writer.

mean: A guide who explains the sights to visitors
story: Eighteenth-century travellers on the Grand Tour hired local guides and named them ciceroni — after Cicero, whose reputation for eloquence had by then drifted into a reputation for not stopping.

mean: Of the emperor Claudius or his period
story: Claudius survived the purges that killed the rest of his family precisely because nobody thought him worth killing. The Praetorian Guard found him hiding behind a curtain after Caligula's murder and made him emperor.

Coleridge said Kubla Khan came to him complete in a dream, and that he was writing it down when a person from Porlock knocked on the door about business. By the time he got rid of the visitor, the rest of the poem was gone.

mean: Of the conflict between passion and duty
story: Corneille's Le Cid was so popular that the French Academy was pushed to condemn it for breaking the rules of classical drama. Audiences kept going anyway, and the phrase beau comme le Cid entered the language.
Cromwell told his portrait painter to include everything, warts and all, or he would not pay for it. Two years after his death the restored monarchy dug up his body and executed it anyway.

mean: Of Delos or the Delian League
story: Delos was so sacred that no one was allowed to be born or to die on it. There is also the Delian problem: an oracle demanded the islanders double a cube-shaped altar, which turns out to be impossible with compass and straightedge.
Western theatre started as a religious festival for Dionysus. The plays of Sophocles and Euripides were competition entries, performed once, in an open-air theatre, at a party for the god of wine.

Asked why the penalty for minor theft was death, Draco reportedly said small crimes deserved it and he could find nothing worse for the large ones. The laws were said to be written in blood rather than ink.

mean: Of the 1900s in Britain; elegant and leisured
story: Edward waited fifty-nine years to become king — the longest apprenticeship in British history — and reigned nine. The decade named after him is remembered as one long garden party, mainly because of what came next.

Elizabeth reigned forty-four years and refused to marry throughout, telling Parliament she was already married to England. The theatre, the language and the navy all took their modern shape while she was on the throne.

mean: Achieving change by patient gradual steps
story: The Fabian Society, founded in 1884, chose the name deliberately: change by patience, not revolution. Its members included George Bernard Shaw and H. G. Wells, and it helped found the British Labour Party.

The Fianna were mythical hunter-warriors who roamed Ireland in the old stories. When republicans organised in 1858 they reached back two thousand years for a name, which tells you how they wanted to be seen.

Gaul gave French a great deal: Gallic wit, Gallicanism, and the rooster that is still France's unofficial emblem — because gallus is Latin for both a Gaul and a cockerel, and someone enjoyed the pun enough to keep it.

The Jacobins were named after a building, not a person — the Paris convent where they met. Under Robespierre the club drove the Terror, and Jacobin has meant dangerous radicalism in English ever since.

mean: Of the reign of James I
story: The King James Bible was produced under him by six committees of scholars, and its cadences shaped English prose for four centuries. Jacobean drama went the other way entirely — revenge, poison and skulls.
Judaea is named for Judah, one of the twelve tribes, whose emblem was a lion. The name travelled: from the tribe to the kingdom to the Roman province, and from there into the word Jewish.

mean: Of Napoleon; boldly ambitious in scale
story: Napoleon's civil code is still the backbone of the legal system in dozens of countries. He was of perfectly ordinary height for his time — the short-Napoleon story comes from British cartoons and a confusion between French and English inches.

mean: Of the apostle Paul or his teaching
story: Paul began as Saul, a persecutor of Christians, and changed course after a blinding experience on the road to Damascus. A Damascene conversion — a sudden complete reversal — is named from that same journey.

mean: An early photograph on a silvered plate
story: The French government bought Daguerre's process in 1839 and gave it to the world free — except in England, where he patented it. Each daguerreotype was unique: there was no negative, so no copies could be made.

mean: A roof with a steep lower slope, giving attic space
story: Paris property was once taxed by the number of floors below the roofline, so a mansard roof added a whole storey the tax collector did not count. Good architecture and good accounting at the same time.

Morse was a portrait painter first. Away from home on a commission, he received a letter saying his wife was ill; by the time he got back she was already buried. He spent the rest of his life on faster messages.

mean: Fabric woven in an intricate pattern on a Jacquard loom
story: Jacquard's loom read its pattern from a chain of punched cards. Charles Babbage saw one and borrowed the idea for his calculating engine, and punched cards ran computers into the 1970s. Modern computing starts with a French silk loom.

Dobermann collected taxes in a rough district and also ran the local dog pound, which gave him unusual access to breeding stock. He set out to build the perfect bodyguard, and the breed still carries his name.

mean: A hairstyle with the hair swept up from the forehead
story: Madame de Pompadour was the most powerful woman at Versailles without being queen, and set fashion for two decades. Two centuries later Elvis Presley wore a version of her hairstyle, which she would probably have enjoyed.

mean: A white sauce of milk thickened with flour and butter
story: Bechameil was a wealthy court official, not a cook. Another courtier complained that the man was lucky — he himself had been serving the same sauce for years before Bechameil was born, and nobody had named it after him.

mean: A soft creamy cheese with a white rind
story: The story goes that Marie Harel sheltered a priest fleeing the French Revolution, and he taught her a cheesemaking method from Brie. The round wooden box came later, and is why Camembert could travel.
Only cheese ripened in the caves of one specific village may be called Roquefort — a protection first granted by royal charter in 1411, making it one of the oldest brand protections in the world.

mean: A fine brandy from the Cognac region
story: All cognac is brandy, but only brandy from around this one town may be called cognac. The rule is strict enough that even neighbouring Armagnac, made a hundred miles away, has to use its own name.

mean: Sparkling wine from the Champagne region
story: The region's name comes from the Latin campania, meaning open country. The bubbles were originally an accident and considered a fault — the cold Champagne winters stopped fermentation, which restarted in spring inside the sealed bottle.

mean: A deep purplish red; wine from Burgundy
story: Burgundy is one of a small group of colours named after drinks — along with claret and port. The region itself is named for the Burgundians, a Germanic people who settled there around 1,500 years ago.

Europeans spent centuries trying to work out how the Chinese made porcelain so thin that light passed through it. The recipe was finally cracked in Saxony in 1708, but by then the tableware was permanently called china.

mean: A rich patterned fabric woven with a reversible design
story: Damascus gave English three words: damask for the cloth, damascene for patterned steel and inlaid metal, and damson for the plum. All three arrived along the same trade routes.

Your jeans are named after two European cities at once. The fabric is de Nimes, from Nimes in France. The trousers are from Genoa in Italy, which the French called Genes — which English turned into jeans.

mean: Very fine soft wool from the cashmere goat
story: Cashmere is not the goat's outer coat but the soft underlayer it grows for winter, combed out by hand in spring. One goat yields a few ounces a year, which is why a cashmere jumper costs what it does.

mean: Wool from the angora goat or rabbit
story: Angora names three different animals — a goat, a rabbit and a cat — all long-haired, all from around Ankara. Confusingly, the goat's wool is sold as mohair, and only the rabbit's is sold as angora.

mean: A lightweight loosely woven cotton cloth
story: The finest muslin actually came from Bengal, where weavers produced cloth so sheer it was nicknamed woven air. Europeans met it in Mosul first, so the Iraqi city got the credit and the name.
Calico was so popular in England that in 1721 Parliament banned it outright to protect the wool trade. The ban lasted thirty-three years and made smuggling printed cotton genuinely profitable.
Marocain is simply French for Moroccan. It is one of several fabrics that arrived in Europe with a nationality attached and kept it, alongside morocco leather from the same country.

mean: A fine leather, originally from Cordoba
story: Cordoba's leather was so famous that the workers who made shoes from it were called cordwainers — a word still used for shoemakers in Britain, six centuries after the trade with Spain dried up.

mean: Leather with a soft napped finish
story: Suede is just the French word for Sweden. Parisians bought Swedish gloves made from the underside of the skin rather than the smooth outer face, and English took the country's name for the texture.

mean: A mountain plant with vivid blue flowers
story: Gentius lost his kingdom to Rome and was paraded through the streets as a captive. His one lasting monument is a small blue alpine flower, named because he supposedly found a use for its extraordinarily bitter root.

mean: A garden plant with small blue or red flowers
story: De l'Obel tried to classify plants by the shape of their leaves, which was wrong but useful — it was one of the first attempts to sort plants by their structure rather than by whether they were edible.

mean: A shrub with bright autumn foliage and berries
story: The name means good name or lucky name — given precisely because the plant is poisonous to cattle. Farmers named it something pleasant in the hope of not attracting bad luck. It is also called the spindle tree.

mean: A garden plant with funnel-shaped flowers
story: Petunia is not named after a person or a place but after a plant it merely resembles. Petun is the Tupi word for tobacco, and petunias and tobacco really are close relatives — both in the nightshade family.

mean: A knitted garment; a breed of dairy cow
story: Jersey knitting was originally what fishermen wore. The island also gave its name to a small fawn-coloured cow prized for creamy milk, and to a large American state that needed a name in 1664.

mean: A smooth linen or cotton fabric
story: Holland cloth was the standard lining and window-blind fabric for centuries. The region also gave English the Dutch oven, Dutch courage and going Dutch — mostly coined by the English during periods of naval rivalry.

mean: A thin crinkled silk or crepe fabric
story: Georgette is one of very few fabrics named after a woman, and one of fewer still named by first name rather than surname. The crinkle comes from twisting the yarn hard in opposite directions before weaving.
Valenciennes lace was so slow to make that a skilled worker might produce an inch and a half in a day, and only in a cool damp cellar — dry air made the linen thread snap.
An arras hung a little away from the wall, which made it useful for eavesdropping. Polonius hides behind one in Hamlet to listen in, and Hamlet stabs straight through the cloth.

mean: Inlaid with wavy patterns; or a sudden total change of view
story: Damascene carries two unrelated senses from the same city: watered patterns in steel, and a Damascene conversion — a sudden reversal of belief, from the apostle Paul's experience on the road there.
Damson is Damascus worn down by centuries of English mouths: damascenum, damascene, damson. The Romans carried the tree west, and it grows in English hedgerows now as if it had always been there.

mean: A thick cold sauce of egg yolk and oil
story: The usual story credits the Duke of Richelieu's cook, improvising a sauce after taking Port Mahon in 1756. Rival theories point to the town of Bayonne or to the French word for egg yolk. Nobody can settle it.

Bologna's own mortadella is studded with pistachios and cubes of fat. The American version dropped nearly all of that, kept the name, and pronounced it baloney — which then became a word for nonsense.

mean: A hard, sharp, aged Italian cheese
story: Real Parmigiano-Reggiano ages at least a year, and each wheel is tested by a man who taps it with a small hammer and listens. Wheels that sound wrong inside are marked and sold under a different name.

mean: A firm smooth Italian cheese, often smoked
story: Provolone means big provola. It is a pasta filata cheese — the curd is heated and stretched like dough until it turns glossy, the same technique that makes mozzarella, then hung in ropes to age.

Madeira was discovered to taste better after crossing the tropics twice in a hot ship's hold. Producers began heating it deliberately. American revolutionaries toasted the Declaration of Independence with it.

Havana cigars are rolled from tobacco grown in the Vuelta Abajo valley, where the soil and humidity are considered impossible to reproduce. Rollers traditionally worked while a reader read novels aloud to the room.

mean: A soft white mineral used for tobacco pipes
story: Not named for a person or a place but for what sailors thought it was: lumps of white mineral washing up light enough to float, so obviously sea foam gone solid. It carves beautifully, which is why pipes were made of it.

mean: A thin smoked sausage; a hot dog
story: Frankfurt has been making this sausage since the 1400s. German emigrants brought it to America, where it met a bread roll — and the frankfurter became the hot dog, named by someone who thought the shape looked like a dachshund.

Vienna and Frankfurt both claim the sausage, and each named it after the other city: Austrians call it a Frankfurter, Germans call it a Wiener. The man who first made it had trained in Frankfurt and moved to Vienna.

Before 1842 nearly all beer was dark and cloudy. Plzen's brewers dumped thirty-six barrels of bad beer in the street, hired a Bavarian brewer, and produced a clear golden lager. Most beer in the world today is a copy of it.
Munster is a worn-down form of monasterium, the Latin for monastery — so the cheese is really called monastery cheese. Irish Munster is a different word entirely, from an old Irish tribal name.

mean: A soft cheese with a very strong smell
story: Limburger's smell comes from a bacterium that also lives on human skin. Researchers have shown that mosquitoes attracted to human feet are equally attracted to a piece of Limburger, which says something about both.

mean: A mild Dutch cheese in a red wax coating
story: Edam ages slowly and barely spoils, which made it the standard cheese for long sea voyages. Dutch ships carried it worldwide, and its red wax shell is really just very effective packaging.
Gouda is named for a marketplace, not a dairy. The town held the sole right to trade cheese in the region, so every wheel that passed through took the town's name regardless of which farm made it.
Cheddar Gorge's caves stay at a steady cool temperature all year, which is exactly what the cheese needs. Cheddar is now the most-eaten cheese in the world, and almost none of it comes from Cheddar.

Stilton is named after a village where it was never produced. Coaches on the Great North Road stopped at the Bell Inn there, the landlord sold cheese from Leicestershire to passengers, and they named it after the stop.

Lea and Perrill mixed the first batch, tasted it, hated it, and left the barrel in the cellar. Eighteen months later they tried it again out of curiosity. Fermentation had transformed it, and they started selling it immediately.

mean: A very hot sauce made from tabasco peppers
story: Tabasco sauce has been made on the same Louisiana island since 1868, aged three years in oak barrels with salt from the salt dome beneath. The pepper — and therefore the name — came from Mexico.

mean: An aromatic bitters used in drinks
story: Dr Siegert made his bitters as medicine for Simon Bolivar's troops. The town changed its name to Ciudad Bolivar in 1846 and the company later moved to Trinidad, so the bottle now names a place that no longer exists.
Giovanni Maria Farina created his scent in Cologne and wrote that it reminded him of an Italian spring morning after rain. His company still exists — arguably the oldest perfume house in the world.

The dye was discovered in the same year as the Battle of Magenta and named to ride the news. It is one of the four printing inks — every colour photo ever printed uses a colour named after a battlefield.
Solferino's real legacy is not the colour. A Swiss traveller named Henry Dunant saw forty thousand casualties left untended after the battle, wrote a book about it, and founded the Red Cross.
Bermuda shorts began as British army tropical kit and became ordinary office wear on the island — worn with a jacket, tie and knee socks. It is still normal business dress in Bermuda.

mean: Heavy cotton twill; trousers made from it
story: Genoese sailors wore trousers of this hard-wearing cloth, and the French called the city Genes. English heard jean. The cloth in modern jeans is denim, from Nimes, so the garment is named after two cities at once.

mean: Printed glazed cotton with a floral pattern
story: Chintz is a rare case of an English singular made from a foreign plural — chints was the plural of chint. It was so fashionable, then so common, that chintzy came to mean cheap and gaudy.

mean: A checked or striped cotton cloth
story: Gingham was originally striped, not checked — the checks arrived later in Manchester mills. The name is Malay, one of a handful of everyday English words that came by ship from Southeast Asia.

Kersey is a village of a few hundred people that named a cloth traded across medieval Europe. Along with worsted from Norfolk, it is a reminder that English wool towns once set the standard for the continent.

mean: Smooth yarn or cloth made from long combed wool
story: Worstead is now a quiet village, but in the Middle Ages its cloth funded the enormous churches that still stand across Norfolk — buildings far too large for the parishes that own them.

mean: A fabric made from angora goat hair
story: Mohair only looks like it contains the word hair. It is Arabic mukhayyar, meaning select cloth, which English speakers reshaped into something that sounded like it made sense. That process is called folk etymology.
Morocco leather was the standard for fine bookbinding for centuries — soft enough to work, strong enough to last. The best grade is still called levant morocco, after another region entirely.

mean: A fine silk or nylon net fabric
story: Tulle is the stuff of every ballet skirt and wedding veil. The town that named it is a quiet place in the Correze that most French people associate with something else entirely — it is also a former presidential hometown.

The Gaza origin is the traditional explanation, though some scholars trace gauze to an Arabic word for raw silk instead. Either way it arrived in Europe along Mediterranean trade routes with its name attached.

Organdy is the crispest cotton made — the stiffness comes from treating the woven cloth with acid. Its name most likely travelled the Silk Road from Urgench, a city few English speakers have ever heard of.

Delft potters were copying Chinese porcelain they could not chemically reproduce, so they faked it: white tin glaze over ordinary clay, painted blue. The imitation became famous in its own right and outlived the thing it imitated.
Majolica is named for a stopover, not a source. The pottery was Spanish, but it reached Italian buyers through Majorca, and Italians named it after the island the ships came from.

Faience and majolica are nearly the same pottery named by two different countries after two different middlemen — the French said Faenza, the Italians said Majorca. Both were describing tin-glazed earthenware.
Porter is named after its drinkers rather than a person or place — the porters who carried loads through London markets. Extra-strong porter was called stout porter, which is where stout comes from.
John Woodhouse's ship sheltered at Marsala, he tasted the local wine, and he added spirit so it would survive the voyage to England. Sicily got an export industry out of one storm.

mean: A fortified wine from southern Spain
story: English merchants heard Jerez, said sherris, assumed the s meant plural, and invented sherry as the singular. The same mistake gave English pea from pease and cherry from cerise.
Claret describes a colour, not a place — the pale red of medieval Bordeaux, which was closer to today's rose. English drinkers kept the word even after the wine got much darker.

mean: A brandy from the Armagnac region
story: Armagnac is older than cognac and distilled only once rather than twice, which leaves more flavour and less polish. It is made in far smaller quantities, largely because Armagnac has no river to the sea.

Panama hats are Ecuadorian. They were shipped through Panama, and when Theodore Roosevelt was photographed wearing one at the canal works in 1906, the wrong name stuck permanently to a hat from another country.

mean: To heat a liquid briefly to destroy harmful microbes
story: Pasteur was asked to find out why French wine kept going sour. He found living organisms in it, and that a short spell at moderate heat killed them without ruining the taste. Milk got the same treatment, and childhood deaths dropped.

mean: A grain crop; breakfast food made from grain
story: Your breakfast is named after a Roman goddess. Ceres governed grain and the harvest, and the Romans called the crops themselves cerealia — her things. Four thousand years later it is written on a cardboard box.

Mercury had winged sandals and never stayed anywhere long. The only liquid metal was named after him for the same reason — it rolls away the moment you touch it. A mercurial person is just as hard to hold.

mean: A mountain that erupts molten rock
story: There is a small Italian island called Vulcano, named for the god the Romans thought was hammering away beneath it. Every volcano on Earth — and on Mars — is named after one god's forge.

mean: Fragments scattered by an exploding shell
story: Shrapnel spent his own money developing the shell and worked on it for years before the army adopted it in 1803. He got a pension and a word in every language. It is not the legacy most people would choose.

mean: Strips of facial hair grown down the sides of the face
story: They were called burnsides first, after the general who wore an enormous pair. Somewhere along the way English swapped the two halves and produced sideburns — which now sounds like it describes the sides, purely by accident.

Duns Scotus was one of the sharpest minds of the Middle Ages. When fashions in learning changed, his stubborn followers were mocked as Dunses — and one of the cleverest men of his age ended up meaning the opposite.

De Sade spent roughly thirty-two years locked up, and wrote much of his work in prison — including one novel on a continuous roll of paper hidden in his cell wall. A psychiatrist coined sadism from his name in 1886.

mean: Taking pleasure in one's own suffering
story: Sacher-Masoch was a respected historian and novelist who deeply resented having his name turned into a clinical term. The psychiatrist Krafft-Ebing coined it anyway, and paired it with sadism in the same book.

mean: A slip in which the first sounds of words are swapped
story: Spooner is supposed to have toasted our queer old dean instead of our dear old queen. Most of the famous examples were probably invented by students, but he really did make the slips — and only ever admitted to one.

mean: A large dark berry crossed from several species
story: Boysen gave up and left his experimental vines to die. Walter Knott tracked down the last few survivors on the abandoned farm, nursed them back, and named the berry after the man who had quit.

mean: A sweet of nuts in caramelised sugar
story: The cook, Clement Lassagne, is said to have invented the sweet after watching a kitchen boy eat spilled caramel and almonds. He named it for his employer, opened a shop, and the shop still exists in Montargis.

mean: A pizza of tomato, mozzarella and basil
story: In 1889 Raffaele Esposito made three pizzas for the visiting queen. She preferred the patriotic one, and he named it after her. Whether the story is strictly true is argued over, but the pizza is definitely named for a queen.

Theobald Smith actually identified the organism. Salmon was his supervisor, and the naming followed the rank rather than the work — an old habit in science. Salmon was the first person in America to earn a veterinary doctorate.

Lister worked out that infection came from invisible organisms and started spraying carbolic acid in operating theatres. Death rates collapsed. He has a bacterium named after him and, less flatteringly, a mouthwash.

mean: A petrol bomb in a bottle
story: Molotov said Soviet aircraft were dropping food to starving Finns. The Finns called the cluster bombs Molotov bread baskets — and named their own petrol bombs Molotov cocktails, a drink to go with the meal.
Geiger's first counters had to be watched, hour after hour, counting flashes on a screen in a dark room. He built the clicking tube partly so that physicists could stop staring and start listening.

Each whole step up the Richter scale is about thirty-two times more energy released — so a magnitude 7 is not slightly worse than a 6, it is thirty-two times worse. Richter built his scale for California and it went worldwide.

The bel turned out to be too big for everyday use, so almost nobody uses it — we use tenths. Bell's mother and wife were both deaf, and his work on sound began as work on teaching deaf children to speak.

mean: A gas burner giving a hot clean flame
story: Peter Desaga, Bunsen's instrument maker, actually built the burner to Bunsen's specification. Bunsen also lost the sight in one eye to an explosion and nearly died twice of arsenic poisoning. Chemistry was more dangerous then.

mean: A shallow lidded dish for growing microbes
story: Before Petri, cultures were grown on plates under bell jars that had to be lifted, letting in whatever was floating past. His two-part dish with an overlapping lid solved contamination with almost no moving parts.

Lynch's court handed out floggings, not hangings — the killing sense came later and much worse. Lynch law began as a phrase for rough frontier justice and turned into a word for one of America's darkest habits.

mean: The first month of the year
story: Janus guarded doorways and had a face on each side, so he could see where you had been and where you were going at the same time. That is exactly what people do on the first of January.

mean: The third month of the year
story: March was once the first month of the Roman year — the point where winter ended and armies could move again. That is also why September, October, November and December mean seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth.

mean: The fifth month of the year
story: Maia was a goddess of growing things, and her month is when growth is at its fastest. She was also the mother of Mercury, which makes May and mercurial distant relatives.

mean: The sixth month of the year
story: Juno looked after marriage, so Romans thought June the luckiest month for a wedding. Two thousand years later June is still the most popular wedding month in much of the world, for a reason almost nobody remembers.

mean: The seventh day of the week
story: Saturday is the odd one out. The Anglo-Saxons swapped most Roman gods for their own — Mars became Tiw, Jupiter became Thor — but nobody found a match for Saturn, so he kept his day.

mean: The fifth day of the week
story: The Romans called it Jupiter's day; the Anglo-Saxons had their own thunder god and swapped him in. In French it is still jeudi, from Jove — so the same day is named after two different thunder gods in two languages.

mean: The sixth day of the week
story: Friday matches Frigg to Venus — love goddess for love goddess. French kept the Roman version as vendredi. English took the Norse one, which is why our week is a mixture of two different mythologies.

mean: The third day of the week
story: Tyr lost his hand feeding it to a giant wolf as a pledge, knowing the pledge was a lie — the bravest act in Norse myth. His day is the plain-sounding Tuesday, which does not hint at any of that.

mean: The fourth day of the week
story: Wednesday is Woden's day, and the silent d is the fossil of the missing name. Odin gave an eye for wisdom and hung from a tree for nine nights to learn the runes — none of which survives in the spelling except that d.

Tuxedo Park is named from a Lenape word, probably meaning something like crooked river. So the most formal jacket in English is named after a New York country club named after a Native American place name.

mean: A low padded seat or footstool without a back
story: An empire that lasted six hundred years is now best known in English homes as a padded footstool. Osman's dynasty ruled from the Balkans to Arabia, and the furniture is what English kept of the name.

One story says his coat-tails caught fire at a fireplace and he simply had them cut off. Another says he lost a bet. Either way the cropped jacket became fashionable and has come back roughly once a century since.

Derrick was a convicted criminal pardoned on condition that he become the hangman. His gallows used a pivoting beam and pulley, and oil rigs use the same shape and the same name four hundred years later.

Ritz was fired from his first restaurant job for being unsuited to the trade. He went on to run the Savoy, open the Paris Ritz, and put his name into English twice — as ritzy and in putting on the Ritz.

mean: A giant redwood tree of California
story: Sequoyah could not read any language when he began, and worked for twelve years to build a writing system from scratch. Within a few years most of the Cherokee nation was literate. The largest trees on Earth carry his name.

mean: A climbing plant with bright papery bracts
story: The plant was probably first described by Jeanne Baret, the expedition's botanist's assistant, who sailed disguised as a man and became the first woman to circumnavigate the globe. The plant is named after the captain.

mean: A small brightly coloured freshwater fish
story: The guppy had already been described and named twice before Guppy sent his specimens, so his name is not the official scientific one. It is the one everybody actually uses, which he probably would have settled for.

mean: A dark red berry crossed from blackberry and raspberry
story: Logan was trying to breed better blackberries and planted his varieties too close to a raspberry. The bees did the rest. He was a judge by profession and got a fruit named after him for a gardening mistake.

mean: A small sweet seedless citrus fruit
story: Brother Clement ran an orphanage outside Oran and noticed one tree in the garden producing unusually sweet, seedless fruit. It was a chance hybrid. Every clementine sold today descends from that single accidental tree.

mean: A seedless variety of mandarin orange
story: The wife of an American ambassador sent trees home from Satsuma province in 1878 and the name travelled with them. In Japan the same fruit is called mikan — nobody there calls it a satsuma.
Tangerines are named for the port they were shipped from, not where they grew — the fruit is originally Chinese. It is the same pattern as the Panama hat: the name records the harbour, not the home.

Cantalupo means something like wolf-song. The melon came from Armenia by way of a papal garden, and the sweet orange fruit in your fruit salad is named after a place where wolves were once heard howling.

mean: A large brass instrument coiled around the player
story: Sousa wanted a bass instrument that would carry sound over a marching band rather than up into the sky. He wrote The Stars and Stripes Forever too, so he is one of very few people who named both an instrument and an anthem.

mean: An electronic instrument played without contact
story: Theremin invented his instrument by accident while building a proximity sensor. He later designed a Soviet listening device that hung inside the American embassy for seven years, powered by nothing but the radio beam aimed at it.

Stradivari made about 1,100 instruments and around 650 survive. Scientists have tested the varnish, the wood density, even the effect of a colder climate on the trees, and still cannot agree on why they sound the way they do.

mean: A piano made by Steinway and Sons
story: Steinweg built his first piano in his kitchen in Germany as a wedding gift for his wife. He emigrated in 1850, changed the name to Steinway because it sounded better in English, and the firm holds well over a hundred patents.

Moog started out building theremin kits as a teenager. His synthesizer reached the public through a 1968 album of Bach played entirely on it, which went platinum and put an electronic instrument in ordinary living rooms.

mean: The SI unit of electric charge
story: Coulomb measured forces far too small to feel by hanging a rod from a fine thread and watching how far it twisted. The same delicate trick was later used to weigh the Earth.

Faraday left school at thirteen and worked as a bookbinder, reading the books he was binding. He became the greatest experimentalist of the century, and turned down both a knighthood and the presidency of the Royal Society.
Maxwell's four equations showed that light is an electromagnetic wave — arguably the single greatest leap in physics between Newton and Einstein. Einstein kept a photograph of him on his study wall.

mean: The SI unit of absorbed radiation dose
story: Gray worked out how to measure exactly how much radiation a tissue absorbs — the difference between a useful cancer treatment and a lethal exposure. It is a rare unit that is genuinely a matter of life and death.

mean: A unit of length equal to one ten-billionth of a metre
story: An angstrom is about the width of a hydrogen atom, which makes it the natural ruler for anything atomic. Angstrom also found hydrogen in the Sun, using nothing but the colours in its light.

mean: The ratio of speed to the speed of sound
story: Mach photographed a bullet in flight in 1887 and captured the shock wave coming off it — the first evidence anyone had seen. Mach 1 is not a fixed speed: sound travels slower in cold air, so it changes with altitude.

mean: A scale of wind force from 0 to 12
story: Beaufort's scale needed no instruments at all — each step is described by what the sea and the sails are doing. Force 12 was originally defined as that which no canvas could withstand.

Asked who owned the patent, Salk said the people did — could you patent the sun? Forgoing the patent may have cost him billions. Polio cases in the United States fell from around 58,000 a year to almost none.

mean: An abdominal thrust to dislodge a blocked airway
story: Heimlich published the technique in 1974 and it was in use within weeks. He was ninety-six when he reportedly used it himself for the first time in an emergency, on a fellow resident of his retirement home.

mean: A quick health score given to newborn babies
story: Apgar wrote her five checks on a scrap of paper in a hospital cafeteria when a student asked how to assess a newborn quickly. It is now performed on virtually every baby born in a hospital anywhere.

mean: A diagram of overlapping circles showing set relations
story: Venn called them Eulerian circles and never claimed to have invented them — versions appear centuries earlier. He did build a cricket bowling machine that clean bowled a visiting Australian team, which he may have preferred to be known for.

mean: The international prizes funded by Nobel's estate
story: A French paper mistakenly printed Nobel's obituary while he was alive, under the headline The Merchant of Death Is Dead. He read his own reputation, disliked it, and rewrote his will to fund the prizes.

mean: An American prize for journalism and writing
story: Pulitzer arrived in America as a penniless immigrant recruited into the Union army, and ended up owning New York's biggest paper. He also helped pay for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal by shaming his readers into donating.
Three people claimed to have named it, all saying the statuette reminded them of someone called Oscar. The Academy could not settle the argument, gave up, and made the nickname official.

Bakelite was the first plastic made from nothing that had ever been alive — no plant, no insect, entirely synthetic. Baekeland had already made a fortune inventing photographic paper, and could afford to experiment.

mean: A long-distance race of about 42 kilometres
story: The modern distance was set at the 1908 London Olympics so the race could start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box — which is why every marathon since has been an oddly specific 42.195 kilometres.

mean: A place of learning or a society of scholars
story: Plato's school met in an olive grove sacred to a half-forgotten hero named Akademos. It ran for nearly nine hundred years, and every academy, academic and academia traces back to that one patch of ground.
Medieval English pronounced Magdalene as maudlin, which is why two Oxford and Cambridge colleges spelled Magdalen are still said that way. Centuries of paintings of her in tears did the rest.

mean: A song of praise or triumph
story: Paean was the doctor who patched the gods up when they were wounded in battle. The hymns sung to him in gratitude gave English the word for any outburst of praise.

Pullman built a whole company town for his workers, then cut wages without cutting rents. The strike that followed in 1894 shut down railways nationwide. He was buried under concrete to stop anyone digging him up.
Hansom was an architect who designed a cab as a sideline, sold the patent for £10,000 and was never paid. The cab made London's streets fast; he went back to designing churches.

Brougham was a lawyer, a Lord Chancellor and a campaigner against slavery, and he is remembered for a carriage. He also popularised Cannes as a resort, more or less by accident, after being stranded there.

mean: A carriage with a folding hood
story: The landau's roof splits in the middle and folds both ways, so passengers could be seen in fine weather and covered in bad. British royal processions still use them for exactly that reason.

mean: A light open carriage; a reckless driver
story: Phaethon took the reins of the sun for one day and nearly destroyed the world before Zeus shot him down. Naming a fast, unstable, open carriage after him was a joke that everyone at the time understood.

mean: A stiff felt hat with a curled brim
story: The future Edward VII visited the spa, liked the hat, and brought it home. Churchill wore one, and so did nearly every diplomat photographed between the wars.

mean: A soft felt hat with an indented crown
story: The novel that gave us the word Svengali also gave us the trilby — named not for the villain but for the heroine, from the hat worn onstage in the first London production.

mean: A hard felt hat with a rounded crown
story: It was commissioned to stop gamekeepers being knocked off their horses by branches. The customer tested the prototype by putting it on the floor and stamping on it. It held, and he paid twelve shillings.

mean: A coiled spring toy that walks downstairs
story: James was designing springs to steady instruments on rough seas when he knocked one off a shelf and watched it step end over end to the floor. His wife found the word slinky in a dictionary.
Rubik built it as a teaching aid and only realised he had made a puzzle when he scrambled it and could not put it back. It took him a month to solve his own invention.
Lego is short for leg godt, Danish for play well. By coincidence it also means I put together in Latin, which the company only discovered later and has been enjoying ever since.

mean: Of dishes named for the singer: peach Melba, Melba toast
story: Escoffier served peach Melba in a swan carved from ice. The toast came later, when the singer was ill and could only manage something very thin and very dry. She got a dessert and a diet food.

mean: A cocktail of peach purée and prosecco
story: Giuseppe Cipriani mixed white peach purée with prosecco at Harry's Bar and thought the colour matched a saint's toga in a Bellini painting. A fifteenth-century artist therefore named a twentieth-century drink.

mean: A cocktail of gin, vermouth and Campari
story: The count had reportedly spent time in America as a rodeo rider and came back wanting something stronger than the drink named after his adopted country. The barman swapped soda for gin, and added an orange slice to mark the difference.

mean: A biscuit with a layer of currants
story: Garibaldi unified Italy and was mobbed by crowds on a visit to England. Britain honoured the liberator of a nation by naming a flat currant biscuit after him, universally known in playgrounds as squashed-fly.

mean: A thick cut of beef tenderloin
story: Chateaubriand was a novelist, ambassador and foreign minister, and is now mostly a steak. His cook grilled the fillet between two lesser cuts so the outer meat burned and the middle stayed perfect, then threw the outer pieces away.

mean: A béchamel sauce enriched with cheese
story: Mornay was a Huguenot leader nicknamed the Pope of the Protestants, who spent his life on theological argument. The attribution of the sauce is shaky, which puts it in good company among French sauces.
Dijon mustard is a recipe, not a place of origin — the name is not protected, so most of it is made elsewhere. The seeds mostly come from Canada, which would surprise a fourteenth-century Burgundian.
Gruyere famously has no holes, despite being the cheese most cartoons draw with them. The holes belong to Emmental, which comes from a different Swiss valley entirely.

mean: A Swiss cheese with large holes
story: The holes are bubbles of carbon dioxide from bacteria, and dairies can control their size by adjusting the temperature. For years the holes got smaller because the milk got cleaner — fewer hay particles for bubbles to form around.

mean: A soft cheese with a white rind
story: At the Congress of Vienna in 1815, with Europe being carved up, the delegates held a competition to name the finest cheese. Brie won, and was dubbed the king of cheeses — the only crown that congress awarded.
Legend says a distracted cheesemaker left curd overnight to chase a girl, added fresh curd in the morning to hide the lapse, and invented a blue cheese. Every blue cheese has a version of this story.
Not a place or a person — pecorino just means sheepish, in the literal sense. Roman legionaries were issued a daily ration of it, which makes it one of the oldest recorded packed lunches.

Mozzarella is named after the action that makes it: the curd is heated, stretched like dough, and pinched off in lumps. The name means the cutting-off, which is exactly what the cheesemaker's hands are doing.
Bolivia is one of very few countries named after a real person. Bolivar liberated six nations and died poor and disillusioned, writing that he who serves a revolution ploughs the sea.
Columbus never set foot in Colombia. The name was chosen by a revolutionary who wanted a title for the whole of Spanish America, and it ended up attached to one country.

Named in 1543 for a Spanish prince who never visited. There have been serious proposals to change it since independence, on the grounds that the country is named after a foreign monarch who colonised it.

Tasman called it Van Diemen's Land after his sponsor. The name was changed in 1856 partly to shake off its association with convict transportation — so the island is named after the navigator instead of the governor.

mean: Island nation in the Indian Ocean
story: A hundred and fifteen islands in the Indian Ocean are named after a French finance minister who never saw them. He was in office for two years and is remembered nowhere else.

Martin Waldseemuller printed the name on a map in 1507 because Vespucci had argued it was a new continent rather than Asia. He later changed his mind and removed it — but a thousand copies were already out.
The bird is named after the islands, and the islands are named after dogs — canis in Latin. So a small yellow songbird is, at two removes, named after a pack of large dogs.

The bird is American and the name is a mistake. English traders met a similar African bird sold by Turkish merchants and called it turkey; when the American bird arrived it inherited the wrong name. The Turkish for it is hindi, meaning Indian.

Euler gave us the symbols e, i, f(x) and the sigma for sums. He also wrote the equation many mathematicians call the most beautiful there is, tying together five fundamental constants in seven characters.

mean: Of a process with no memory of its past
story: Markov developed his chains partly to win an argument, analysing the vowels and consonants in a Pushkin poem to prove a rival wrong about probability. The maths now runs speech recognition and page ranking.

Mandelbrot asked how long the coast of Britain is, and answered: it depends on the length of your ruler. Measure in smaller steps and it gets longer without limit. That question opened up fractal geometry.

Hamilton solved a problem he had wrestled with for years while walking along a Dublin canal, and carved the formula into the stone of Broom Bridge with a penknife. A plaque marks the spot; mathematicians still visit.

mean: Of a group where the order of operations does not matter
story: Abel proved that no formula can solve every fifth-degree equation, settling a question three centuries old. He died of tuberculosis at twenty-six, two days before a letter arrived offering him a professorship.

mean: The SI unit of radiation dose equivalent
story: A gray measures energy absorbed; a sievert measures how much harm it does, which depends on the kind of radiation. The difference matters: the same energy from alpha particles is twenty times more damaging.

mean: A unit of magnetic field strength
story: Orsted spotted it during a lecture, in front of students, when a compass on the bench moved as he switched on a current. He said nothing at the time and spent three months checking before publishing.

mean: A unit of pressure, one millimetre of mercury
story: Torricelli filled a tube with mercury, upended it in a dish, and found the column always fell to about the same height — leaving a vacuum above it. Philosophers had insisted for two thousand years that a vacuum was impossible.
The word appears suddenly in London newspapers in the summer of 1898, already meaning street rowdy. Whether the Houlihans were a real family, a music-hall joke, or both, nobody has ever settled.

The Luddites were not against machines in principle — they were skilled workers whose trade was being destroyed and who had no vote to object with. Ned Ludd, in whose name they wrote, probably never existed.

mean: Of wildly exaggerated tales; a disorder involving feigned illness
story: The real baron told entertaining war stories. A writer published a wildly embroidered version without asking, making him a laughing stock across Europe — he spent his last years trying to sue, and hated the book.

mean: A rum, lime and sugar cocktail
story: Jennings Cox ran out of gin while entertaining guests near the Daiquiri mines and improvised with local rum. Hemingway later drank them in Havana by the dozen, and had a variant named after him in turn.

mean: A cocktail of whiskey and vermouth
story: The island's own name comes from a Lenape word usually translated as place where we get bows, after the wood that grew there. So the drink is named after an island named after a bow-making forest.

mean: A tequila, lime and orange-liqueur cocktail
story: At least six people have claimed to have invented it for a woman named Margarita. The likelier answer is dull: daisy was already a category of cocktail, and margarita is simply the Spanish for daisy.

Hooley noticed a stretch of road outside an ironworks that was smooth and dustless, and learned a tar barrel had burst there and been covered with slag. He patented the accident and named it after McAdam.

Walton got the idea from the rubbery skin that forms on a tin of old paint. He never trademarked the name, and a court ruled in 1878 that it had already become generic — the first product ever to lose a name that way.

mean: A ship's load line; a rubber-soled canvas shoe
story: Plimsoll campaigned against coffin ships — overloaded and over-insured vessels worth more sunk than afloat. The shoe is named after the line too: the rubber band round the sole looks just like a ship's load mark.

Sabin's vaccine could be swallowed rather than injected, which made mass campaigns possible in places with few doctors. Like Salk, he refused to patent it. The two men disliked each other for decades.

Wurlitzer organs were built to replace whole orchestras in silent-film theatres — one player, hundreds of pipes, plus drums, cymbals, birdsong and a car horn. Sound film arrived and the market vanished almost overnight.

Gibson had no formal training and carved instrument tops from a single piece of wood, arched like a violin, when everyone else bent flat sheets. He sold the patent and the company outgrew him entirely.

Fender never learned to play the guitar. He was a radio repairman who approached the instrument as an engineering problem — bolt the neck on so it can be replaced, and the whole thing can be built on a production line.

mean: To keep something to oneself instead of sharing
story: To bogart something is to hog it, from the way Bogart kept a cigarette clamped in his mouth without ever seeming to smoke it. The word entered wide use through a 1968 song.

mean: A trailing houseplant with striped leaves
story: The Tradescants kept a museum of curiosities in Lambeth called the Ark, open to anyone who paid sixpence — the first public museum in England. Its collection became the founding core of Oxford's Ashmolean.

mean: A yellow daisy-like flower, the black-eyed Susan
story: Rudbeck discovered the lymphatic system as a student, and later spent decades trying to prove that Sweden was the lost Atlantis. Linnaeus named the flower for him regardless.

mean: A flowering tree, extinct in the wild
story: The Bartrams found this tree growing in one small patch in Georgia in 1765 and collected seeds. It has not been seen in the wild since 1803. Every franklinia alive today descends from those seeds.
Its other name is dumb cane: the sap contains needle-shaped crystals that make the mouth and throat swell, temporarily robbing anyone who chews it of speech. It remains a popular office plant.

mean: A shade plant grown for its leaves
story: Hostas are grown for foliage rather than flowers, thrive in shade, and are eaten enthusiastically by slugs. Host himself was physician to the Austrian emperor and ran the imperial botanical garden.
Alfred Butts, an out-of-work architect, counted letter frequencies on the front page of the New York Times to set the tile values. The game failed twice under other names before Scrabble stuck.

Leslie Scott's family played it with wooden blocks from a sawmill in Ghana. She named it from the Swahili kujenga, to build — which is slightly ironic for a game everyone plays in order to watch it fall over.

Elizabeth Magie invented the original in 1904 as a protest against landlords hoarding property. Decades later a man sold a version to Parker Brothers as his own invention. She was paid five hundred dollars.

Sousa wrote The Stars and Stripes Forever, the official national march of the United States. He also campaigned against recorded music, warning it would stop people learning instruments — a prediction with some merit.
A Borsalino takes around seven weeks and dozens of separate operations to make, mostly from rabbit felt. The firm was still going after more than 160 years, which very few hat companies can say.

Listerine was sold first as a surgical antiseptic, then as a floor cleaner and a cure for gonorrhoea. It only became a mouthwash when the makers popularised the word halitosis to convince people they had a problem.

mean: A patty of minced beef served in a bun
story: Sailors leaving one busy German port ate a minced beef steak served flat on a plate. They carried the habit across the Atlantic, cooks there slid the patty into a bun, and the sandwich kept the port city's name.

mean: A team sport played with an oval ball that players may carry
story: At one English school the football rules allowed a player to pick the ball up and run with it. Old boys carried the handling version to clubs everywhere, and to tell it apart from the kicking game people simply called it by the school's name.

mean: A white dog covered in black or brown spots
story: A tall spotted dog that loved to trot beside horses became fashionable as a carriage escort. Early writers linked the breed to one stretch of Adriatic coastline, and although the connection is thin, the region's name stuck to the dog for good.

mean: A strong, friendly retriever with a short water-shedding coat
story: Fishermen on a cold Canadian coast kept short-haired dogs that dived into freezing water after nets and fish. English gentlemen brought the dogs home, bred them for the shooting field, and named them after the coast they came from.

mean: A very small dog with large upright ears
story: American visitors to a northern Mexican state in the 1800s bought tiny dogs from villagers near the border. Nobody recorded a breed name, so the buyers simply used the name of the state, and the smallest dog in the world has answered to it since.

mean: A soft round fruit with fuzzy skin and a large stone
story: The fruit really began in China, but it reached Rome along the road from Persia. Roman growers called it the Persian apple, persicum, and centuries of shortening in French wore that long name down to a single soft syllable.

mean: A hot drink brewed from roasted ground beans
story: Wild bushes with red berries still grow in one Ethiopian highland. Traders carried the beans to Arabia, where the brewed drink became qahwa, and every European name for it -- cafe, kaffee and the English word -- goes back to that first green hillside.

mean: A very large expanse of salt water
story: Greeks imagined the earth as a flat disc ringed by one endless river, and gave that river the name of a titan, the eldest son of sky and earth. When sailors learned the water went on much further than they thought, the titan's name went with it.

mean: A device that makes a loud wailing warning sound
