story: In the old story, singers on a rocky island sang so beautifully that crews steered towards them and were wrecked. Odysseus tied himself to the mast to hear them safely. Centuries later an inventor gave the name to a machine whose wail means danger.

mean: Someone overlooked who suddenly rises to success
story: A girl who slept beside the fireplace and was named for the cinders in her clothes went to the ball and left one slipper behind. Now any unfancied team that reaches the final, or any ignored talent that shines, gets called by her name.

mean: Neither too much nor too little; just right
story: A girl in a fairy tale tried porridge too hot, then too cold, then just right. Astronomers borrowed her fussiness: a planet in the narrow band that is neither too hot nor too cold for water now sits in the zone named for her.

mean: A resort with mineral springs or health treatments
story: A Belgian town with bubbling iron-rich springs became the fashionable place to take the waters in the 1500s. Visitors came home saying they had been to the town by name, and soon every mineral bath in Europe was borrowing it.

mean: A small oily fish often packed tightly in tins
story: Fishing boats around one large Mediterranean island hauled in silver shoals of a small oily fish by the tonne. The catch was salted, shipped and eventually tinned, and it carried the island's name to breakfast tables everywhere.

mean: A racket game played with a shuttlecock over a high net
story: Officers home from India brought back a shuttlecock game and played it in the hall of an English duke's country house on a wet afternoon. When people asked what the game was called, they answered with the name of the house.

mean: A blue-green mineral, or that colour
story: The blue-green stone was mined in Persia, but it reached Venice and Paris in the packs of Turkish merchants. French buyers called it pierre turquoise, the Turkish stone, and the shortened word now names the colour as much as the mineral.

mean: A Mexican spirit distilled from blue agave
story: In the red volcanic soil around one Mexican town, blue agave plants grow for years before their hearts are roasted and distilled. Mexican law now says the spirit may only carry the town's name if it comes from that region.

mean: A very small long-haired dog with a plumed tail
story: Big white spitz dogs pulled sleds along a cold Baltic coast. Breeders shrank them generation by generation until Queen Victoria fell for an eleven-pound one and made the miniature fashionable, and the region's name shrank onto the little dog.

mean: A large powerful black-and-tan guard dog
story: Butchers in a German market town used heavy dogs to drive cattle to market, then tied the purse of takings round the dog's neck for the walk home. Nobody robbed them. The town's name went onto the breed and stayed.

mean: A slender pale cat with dark face, ears, paws and tail
story: A pair of pale blue-eyed cats with sooty faces was given to a British consul by a royal court in South East Asia in 1884. They were shown in London the next year, astonished everybody, and took the kingdom's old name as their own.

mean: A rich coffee, or coffee flavoured with chocolate
story: For two hundred years almost every coffee bean that reached Europe left through one Yemeni harbour. The beans had a chocolatey edge, so when cooks later stirred cocoa into coffee they reached for the harbour's name to describe it.

Dutch growers planted coffee across one Indonesian island until it supplied much of the world. American sailors and soldiers took to calling any cup of coffee by the island's name, and a programming language later borrowed it as a nod to the coders' fuel.

mean: A hard-shelled Australian nut with rich creamy flesh
story: A botanist studying rainforest trees in Queensland found one with a nut so hard you needed a hammer. He named the genus after a chemist friend who, as it happens, never tasted the nut that would carry his name around the world.

mean: A grilled sandwich of corned beef, sauerkraut, cheese and dressing on rye
story: A grocer playing his weekly poker game in an Omaha hotel asked the kitchen for corned beef, sauerkraut, Swiss cheese and dressing between rye bread, grilled. The hotel owner put it on the menu under the player's first name, and it never came off.

mean: A layered pastry of puff pastry and cream
story: The layered cream slice began as a Naples pastry, napolitain in French. English speakers heard the more famous name in it and rewrote the word, so the dessert now honours an emperor who had nothing whatever to do with inventing it.

mean: A slow-cooked Italian meat and tomato sauce
story: Cooks in one wealthy northern Italian city simmered minced meat with a little tomato, milk and wine for hours, and served it with wide flat pasta. The city's name travelled with the recipe, though what most countries make of it would horrify the locals.

mean: Ice cream in three coloured layers
story: Ice cream makers from a southern Italian port emigrated in the 1800s and sold moulded ice cream in coloured stripes, in imitation of their national flag. Abroad the layers became chocolate, vanilla and strawberry, and kept the city's name.

mean: A red wine from the region around one French port
story: For centuries English merchants bought red wine at one French Atlantic port and shipped it home in barrels. They called it by the harbour rather than the vineyard, and even now the region's most famous wines answer to the port's name.

mean: A deep blue-violet dye or colour
story: Greek traders met a deep blue dye that came in hard cakes from the East, and called it indikon, simply the Indian thing. The name outlasted the trade: the colour between blue and violet in the rainbow still carries the country's name.

mean: A soft reddish metal that conducts heat and electricity well
story: Rome got most of its reddish metal from mines on one Mediterranean island, and called it the Cyprus metal. Latin wore aes cyprium down to cuprum, and English wore that down again, so an island's name now sits in every electrical cable.

During the First World War British owners could not bring themselves to call the breed a German shepherd. They renamed it after a border region that had changed hands between the two countries, and in Britain the wartime alias lasted for decades.

mean: A small flat-faced dog with a long flowing coat
story: Only the Chinese imperial family could keep the little lion dogs of the palace. When British and French troops looted the Summer Palace in 1860 five were carried off, one was given to Queen Victoria, and the capital's old name went with them.

mean: A horse breed with a dished face, high tail and great stamina
story: Desert tribes bred horses that could go far on little water and live close to the family tent. The line is one of the oldest kept anywhere, and almost every modern racing breed carries some of its blood along with the peninsula's name.

mean: A problem that grows worse each time you attack it
story: Heracles found that every head he sliced off the marsh serpent was replaced by two more, and only fire could stop the regrowth. Ever since, a difficulty that spawns two new difficulties each time you solve it has been called by the monster's name.

mean: A large snake that kills by constriction
story: A monstrous serpent guarded the spring at Delphi until Apollo shot it, and the oracle's priestess took her title from it. When naturalists needed a name for enormous constricting snakes, they reached back into the myth for the serpent's own.

mean: The coloured lights that glow in polar skies
story: Romans said a goddess rose each morning to paint the eastern sky before the sun came up. When Galileo needed a name for the green and red curtains that hang over the far north, he gave them hers, adding the northern dawn.

mean: A person behaving wildly or foolishly
story: Doctors from Rome to the Middle Ages believed that fits of madness rose and fell with the phases of the moon, and English law once separated the permanently ill from those thought to change with it. The moon goddess's name is still inside the word.

mean: American whiskey distilled mainly from corn and aged in charred oak
story: Barrels of corn whiskey floated down the Ohio and Mississippi from one Kentucky county, whose name was stencilled on the staves. By the time they reached New Orleans the oak had mellowed the spirit, and buyers asked for it by the county on the barrel.

mean: A cylindrical canvas bag closed with a drawstring
story: A Belgian town wove a thick coarse wool that soldiers and sailors trusted to keep out weather. Coats and kitbags cut from it carried the town's name across every navy in Europe, and the bag kept the name long after the cloth changed.

mean: A machine that shaves and resurfaces ice
story: Resurfacing a rink took five men over an hour. A rink owner in California spent nine years bolting a shaving blade, a water tank and a squeegee onto an army surplus chassis until one driver could do it in ten minutes. His name is now on the machine everywhere.

An Austrian businessman raced Daimler cars under his young daughter's name because a foreign entrant needed a pseudonym. The cars won, dealers demanded that model by that name, and the factory quietly made a ten-year-old girl's name its own.

mean: An American luxury car; anything of the highest quality
story: A French officer built a fort on a narrow strait and called it the place of the strait, which became Detroit. Two centuries later a carmaker in that city borrowed his name and his family crest, and the word came to mean the best of anything.

A Swiss racing driver went into partnership with an ousted car executive, lending his famous name to a new company. He fell out with his partner over building cheap cars, sold his shares early, and watched his surname become one of the biggest in America.

mean: A blade fixed to the muzzle of a rifle
story: The story goes that soldiers besieged in a French border city ran out of powder and jammed their hunting knives into their musket barrels. Whether or not that happened, the city's forges made the blades, and its name went onto them.

mean: A hard glossy black lacquer finish
story: Lacquered boxes arriving from East Asia in the 1600s astonished Europe with a black finish nothing local could match. Workshops in England and France tried to copy it, sold the results as the country's own name, and turned a nation into a verb.

mean: A close-fitting knitted woollen jumper; also a breed of dairy cow
story: Fishermen on a small Channel Island knitted jumpers so tightly that seawater ran off them. Naval crews adopted the pattern, Australian footballers borrowed the word for their shirts, and the island's dairy cattle carried the same name to farms worldwide.

mean: A very large draught horse with feathered legs
story: Farmers in one Scottish river valley crossed local mares with imported Flemish stallions to get a horse that could haul coal and plough heavy clay. The breed grew to a tonne, kept its white feathered legs, and carried the valley's name to the world.

mean: A small dried grape used in baking
story: Medieval traders bought tiny seedless dried grapes at a Greek port and sold them in England as raisins of that city. The phrase wore down over centuries until only a mangled version of the city's name was left on the packet.

mean: A small mild onion that grows in clusters
story: Returning crusaders brought back a small onion that grew in clusters and tasted milder than the ones at home. They said it came from one Levantine port, called it the onion of that place, and French cooks wore the phrase down to a single word.

mean: A long-tailed game bird with bright plumage
story: Greek sailors returning from the Black Sea brought back a spectacular long-tailed bird and said it lived along one particular river. They called it the bird of the Phasis, and every European language still carries a worn-down version of that river's name.

mean: A warm sauce of egg yolk, butter and lemon
story: French cooks named several sauces after foreign countries to suggest a style rather than an origin. This one, whisked from yolks and warm butter until it thickens, was labelled Dutch, possibly because the Netherlands supplied the butter.

mean: A warm sauce of egg yolk, butter, tarragon and shallot
story: A chef outside Paris invented a herbed butter sauce at a restaurant named for Henry IV, who was born in a Pyrenean region and nicknamed for it. The sauce took the region's name, though nobody there had ever made it.

A grand duke drew a boundary round some Tuscan hills in 1716 and declared that only wine from inside it could carry the region's name. It was one of the first protected wine areas anywhere, three centuries before such rules became normal.

Growers in a French region north of Lyon make a light red from gamay grapes and release the newest vintage on the third Thursday of November. Bottles race to Paris and beyond overnight, and the region's name goes with every cork.

mean: A white wine grape, or the wine made from it
story: A small Burgundy village gave its name to a green-skinned grape that turned out to grow almost anywhere, from Champagne to California to Australia. It is now the most planted white wine grape on earth, still carrying one village's name.

mean: A Spanish red wine aged in oak
story: When disease wrecked French vineyards in the 1800s, Bordeaux winemakers crossed the Pyrenees and taught growers in a northern Spanish valley to age wine in oak barrels. The region kept the technique, and its name now means oak-aged Spanish red.

mean: A loud musical instrument of steam whistles
story: An inventor in 1855 mounted a keyboard on a row of steam whistles loud enough to be heard eight miles away. He named it for the Muse of epic poetry, whose name means beautiful-voiced, which anyone who has stood near a circus one may dispute.

On his last voyage Gulliver meets talking horses ruling over filthy, howling creatures that look uncomfortably like humans. Swift meant it as a mirror. The creatures' name became an insult, and much later a search engine picked it up as a joke.

mean: Deliberately ambiguous or misleading official language
story: In Orwell's novel the state shrinks the dictionary every year, on the theory that a thought you have no word for cannot be thought at all. The invented language's name is now used for any official wording designed to blur rather than explain.

mean: Holding two contradictory beliefs at the same time
story: Orwell's Party required citizens to believe two opposite things at once and to be sincere about both, forgetting the contradiction and then forgetting the forgetting. The coined word escaped the novel and is now used of real politics every week.

mean: A pattern of coloured diamonds; a comic acrobatic character
story: A masked servant character in Italian street comedy wore a patched costume that hardened over time into neat coloured diamonds. He tumbled, schemed and chased Columbine through two centuries of theatre, and left his name on the pattern itself.

In Italian street comedy the servant clowns, named from a dialect form of Giovanni, copied their masters' gestures badly on purpose. English audiences took the troupe's name for the behaviour, and it now describes any cheerfully absurd person.

mean: The lightest inert gas, used to fill balloons
story: During an eclipse in 1868 astronomers saw a yellow line in the sun's spectrum that matched no known element. They named the unknown gas after the Greek sun god. Twenty-seven years passed before anyone found any of it on earth.

An English baronet imported plum trees from a French monastery, and the labels were lost on the way. His gardener, needing something to call the green ones, combined the colour with his employer's surname, and the plum has answered to it since.

A wounded Soviet tank sergeant lay in hospital listening to comrades complain that German troops had better automatic weapons. He sketched a design built to work when filled with mud or sand. Over a hundred million have been made, all carrying his name.

mean: A German bolt-action rifle or pistol
story: A German designer perfected a bolt action so reliable that armies from Spain to Japan bought or copied it, and hunting rifles still use his locking system a century later. His surname is stamped on more military rifles than almost any other.

mean: The matrix of partial derivatives of a vector function
story: A German mathematician studied the grid of partial derivatives that says how much a change of coordinates stretches or twists each direction. Its determinant is the factor by which volume changes, which is why it appears in every multiple integral.

Shepherds on a high plateau in northern Italy once made this cheese from sheep's milk. When cattle replaced the flocks the recipe changed but the name did not, and European law now protects it for that plateau alone.

mean: A mild orange American cheese with a springy texture
story: A Wisconsin cheesemaker's teenage son washed the curds in cold water instead of letting them cook dry, and got a softer, milder, moister cheese than cheddar. It was the first cheese invented in America, and it took the little town's name.

mean: A semi-soft Danish cheese with small holes
story: A Danish woman toured European dairies, came home to an experimental farm outside Copenhagen, and worked out a semi-soft cheese full of tiny irregular holes. The farm's name went onto it, and Denmark's best-known cheese was born on a research plot.

mean: Coated in breadcrumbs and fried, in the style of one Italian city
story: A northern Italian city gave its name to two very different dishes: a veal cutlet beaten thin, breadcrumbed and fried in butter, and a risotto turned gold with saffron. Vienna's schnitzel is very probably the same cutlet under another flag.

mean: Cooked with sliced onions, in the style of one French city
story: One French city is so serious about food that its small restaurants have their own name, bouchons. Any dish labelled with the city's adjective on a French menu comes with sliced onions browned in butter, whatever else is on the plate.

mean: Cooked with tomato, garlic and olive oil
story: The name of a southern French region on a menu promises the same three things every time: tomato, garlic and olive oil, usually with herbs from the dry hills. The region's Roman name simply meant the province, the first one Rome held outside Italy.

mean: Wide or tight trousers, depending on the century
story: A stock character in Italian street comedy played a mean old Venetian merchant in tight full-length hose, unusual when other men wore breeches. Audiences named the garment after him, French shortened it, and the word ended up as plain pants.

mean: A boastful coward; a roguish clown
story: A stock character in Italian comedy strutted in black with a sword, boasted of battles he had not fought, and ran at the first real threat. His name, from a word meaning skirmish, became the English word for exactly that sort of man.

Dickens created an architect who never designed a building, lived off his pupils' work, and lectured everyone he met about virtue while cheating them. His name became the exact English word for moralising that the moraliser has no intention of following.

mean: A genus of tiny bacteria carried by ticks, lice and fleas
story: An American pathologist traced spotted fever to ticks, then went to Mexico to study typhus. He caught it from the lice he was working with and died at thirty-nine. The genus was named for him a few years later.

mean: A genus of bacteria causing severe dysentery
story: During a dysentery epidemic that killed a fifth of those infected, a young Japanese bacteriologist isolated the organism from patients' stools and proved it was the cause. He was twenty-six. Both the genus and the toxin it makes carry his name.

mean: A genus of bacteria causing pneumonia and other infections
story: A German microbiologist who also spotted the diphtheria organism under his microscope gave his name to a genus of rod-shaped bacteria wrapped in a thick slimy capsule. That capsule is exactly what makes them so hard for the immune system to grip.

mean: A genus of bacteria including the cause of plague
story: Two researchers found the plague organism in Hong Kong within days of each other in 1894, and for decades the credit was muddled. The genus now carries the name of the one whose samples were clean, who also worked out that rats and their fleas carried it.

mean: A genus of gut bacteria, one species of which is used in every laboratory
story: A paediatrician studying infant digestion described a rod-shaped bacterium living harmlessly in the gut. It was renamed in his honour after his death, and the species is now the most studied organism on earth after ourselves.

mean: A genus of bacteria causing undulant fever, caught from livestock
story: A Scottish army surgeon posted to Malta traced the fever wrecking the garrison to an organism in goats' milk. Stopping the milk ration ended the epidemic almost overnight, and the genus was named after him.

mean: A chilled soup of leek, potato and cream
story: A French chef working at a New York hotel served the leek and potato soup of his childhood cold instead of hot, on a hot summer day. He named it after the spa town near his home, and a Manhattan invention now sounds thoroughly French.

mean: A grammatical mistake, or a breach of good manners
story: Athenian visitors to a distant Greek colony were appalled by the dialect the settlers had drifted into, and turned the town's name into an insult for any mangled sentence. The word later widened to cover social blunders as well as grammatical ones.

mean: To wander in loops without hurrying; a bend in a river
story: One river in Asia Minor looped so extravagantly across its flat valley that Greek writers used its name as a byword for anything that would not go straight. Geographers still use it as the technical term for a river bend.

mean: A bitter denunciation delivered in public
story: An Athenian orator spent years warning his city about the ambitions of a northern king, in speeches so fierce that the king's name became the word for any blistering public attack. Cicero later borrowed the form to go after Mark Antony.

mean: A long mournful complaint or denunciation
story: A Hebrew prophet warned his city for forty years that disaster was coming, was thrown into a cistern for saying so, and then watched it happen. The book of laments that followed gave English a word for any lengthy, gloomy tirade.

mean: The buying or selling of church office or sacred things
story: A sorcerer watched the apostles lay hands on people and offered them cash for the same power. Peter's refusal was blistering. His name became the church's legal term for buying office, and a serious offence for the next eighteen centuries.

Souls were ferried across one black river to reach the land of the dead, and the gods swore their most binding oaths on its water. Anything gloomy enough to suggest that crossing is described with the river's name.

mean: Tall, stately and imposing, of a woman
story: The Roman queen of the gods was pictured as tall, broad-browed and unmistakably in charge, never girlish. Painters and novelists borrowed her name as a compliment for a woman built on the same commanding scale.

mean: A hall for public lectures, or a school
story: Aristotle taught in a grove outside Athens sacred to Apollo under one of his titles, walking as he lectured. The grove's name became the word for a lecture hall, and in France it still names the secondary school itself.

mean: A person interested only in hard facts and figures
story: Dickens opened a novel with a schoolmaster demanding facts, nothing but facts, and a girl punished for defining a horse poetically instead of anatomically. His name is now the English word for anyone who measures everything and understands nothing.

mean: Hopelessly optimistic about money that never arrives
story: Dickens created a man permanently one letter away from ruin who assured everyone that something would turn up. Economists borrowed his budgeting advice, and his name became the word for waiting for rescue instead of arranging one.

mean: A pistol or machine gun of an American design
story: A gunsmith's son in Utah filed his first patent at twenty-four and ended with a hundred and twenty-eight. He designed the pistol the US Army carried for seventy-four years, and died at his workbench in Belgium with a design half finished.

mean: Of the tube joining the middle ear to the back of the throat
story: An Italian anatomist working before the printing of good anatomical plates described the narrow tube that lets the middle ear equalise pressure. It is why your ears pop in a lift, and it has carried his name for four centuries.

mean: Of the pair of tubes carrying eggs from ovary to womb
story: An Italian anatomist who died at thirty-nine described the delicate tubes running from ovary to womb, comparing their flared ends to trumpets. He got the function wrong but the anatomy right, and the tubes still bear his name.

mean: Of the tiny canals carrying blood vessels through compact bone
story: An English physician put thin slices of bone under an early microscope and found it was not solid at all but drilled through with a network of tiny tunnels carrying blood vessels. Bone turned out to be plumbing, and the canals took his name.

mean: Of the layered receptors deep in skin that sense pressure and vibration
story: An Italian anatomist found onion-layered capsules buried deep in the skin and joints that fire when pressed or vibrated. He also saw the cholera bacterium thirty years before Koch, and got credit for neither in his lifetime.

mean: Of the fluid-filled ovarian follicle that releases a mature egg
story: A Dutch physician described the fluid-filled blisters on the ovary and argued they held the egg. He was nearly right: they hold the follicle that releases it. He died at thirty-two, embittered by a priority quarrel with a colleague.

mean: Of several microscopic structures in kidney, spleen or insect excretory system
story: An Italian microscopist was the first to see capillaries, red blood cells and the filtering knots of the kidney. So much of the invisible body was his discovery that his name now attaches to structures in three separate organ systems.

mean: Of the oil glands lining the rim of the eyelid
story: A German physician described rows of tiny oil glands along the eyelid margin. Their oil stops tears evaporating too fast; when they clog, eyes feel gritty and dry. Modern eye clinics still name the condition after him.

mean: Of the small extra bones sometimes found within skull sutures
story: A Danish physician described the small irregular islands of bone that sometimes form inside the wavy joints of the skull. They are harmless in most people but crowd in on certain bone diseases, which is why radiologists still count them.

mean: Of the deep fissure separating the temporal lobe of the brain
story: A Dutch physician traced the deep cleft that separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes. It is the most obvious landmark on the side of the human brain, and the artery running along it carries his name too.

mean: Of the central furrow of the brain dividing motor from sensory cortex
story: An Italian anatomist mapped the deep furrow running down the top of the brain. In front of it lies the strip that commands movement; behind it, the strip that receives touch. A whole class of childhood epilepsy is named from that furrow.

mean: Of conducting fibres in the heart or large branching neurons in the cerebellum
story: A Czech physiologist who founded the world's first independent physiology department described both the fibres that carry the heart's electrical signal and the huge fan-shaped neurons of the cerebellum. Two entirely different cells carry the same name.

mean: Of the cells that wrap peripheral nerve fibres in an insulating sheath
story: A German physiologist proposed that all animal tissue is built from cells, then found the ones that spiral around nerve fibres like insulation on wire. Without them a nerve signal would crawl instead of race.

mean: Of the stack of membranes that packages proteins inside a cell
story: An Italian physician invented a silver stain that made single nerve cells stand out black against pale tissue. It won him a Nobel Prize shared with a rival he publicly disagreed with, and it revealed the cell's packaging depot, now named for him.

mean: Of the scavenging immune cells lining the liver's blood channels
story: A Baltic German anatomist described star-shaped cells stationed in the liver's blood channels. They swallow bacteria and worn-out red cells as blood filters past, making the liver a checkpoint as well as a chemical works.

mean: Of the nurse cells that support developing sperm cells
story: An Italian physiologist, still a student when he made the discovery, described tall cells in the testis that cradle developing sperm and feed them through their whole maturation. They are among the few true nurse cells in the body.

mean: Of the cells in the testis that produce testosterone
story: A German zoologist described clusters of cells sitting between the sperm-making tubes rather than inside them. Their job turned out to be chemical, not reproductive: they make the hormone that drives male development.

mean: Of the touch-receptor cells at the base of the outer skin layer
story: A German anatomist described cells sitting at the base of the outer skin layer that report steady pressure and fine texture. They are why you can feel the difference between paper and silk with a fingertip.

mean: Of the light-touch receptors just below the skin surface
story: A German anatomist described egg-shaped bundles of nerve endings packed just under hairless skin. They fire on the lightest brush and go quiet if the touch holds still, which is why you stop noticing your own clothes.

mean: Of the receptors that sense sustained stretch in skin and joints
story: An Italian anatomist described spindle-shaped nerve endings that report sustained stretch rather than momentary touch. They tell your brain where your fingers are without your having to look, which is how you can type in the dark.

mean: Of the cup-shaped capsule that collects filtered fluid in the kidney
story: An English surgeon showed that the kidney works by filtering blood through a knot of capillaries into a cup, rather than by secreting urine directly. The cup is named after him and the filtering knot after Malpighi.

mean: Of the hairpin loop in the kidney tubule that concentrates urine
story: A German anatomist traced a hairpin bend in the kidney's tubules that dips down into the organ and back. The bend lets the kidney pull water back out of urine, which is why land animals can survive on so little of it.

mean: Of the patches of immune tissue in the wall of the small intestine
story: A Swiss anatomist described oval patches of immune tissue studding the lining of the small intestine. They sample everything passing through, which makes them the gut's border control and the first place typhoid attacks.

mean: Of the glands in the duodenum that secrete protective alkaline mucus
story: A Swiss anatomist described glands in the first stretch of intestine that pump out alkaline mucus. Their job is defensive: they neutralise the flood of stomach acid before it can burn the gut wall downstream.

mean: Of the nerve network in the gut wall that drives its muscular waves
story: A German neuropathologist found a full nerve network woven between the muscle layers of the gut. It runs the waves that push food along without asking the brain, which is why the gut is sometimes called a second nervous system.

mean: Of the brain region essential for understanding language
story: A German neurologist found patients who spoke fluently in complete nonsense and could not understand a word said to them. The damage sat behind the ear, in a region that turns sound into meaning, and it carries his name.

mean: Of the brain region essential for producing fluent speech
story: A French physician examined a patient who understood everything but could say only one syllable. The autopsy showed a lesion in the left frontal lobe. It was the first hard evidence that a single mental function lives in one patch of brain.

mean: Of the sensory organ of the inner ear that turns sound into nerve signals
story: An Italian anatomist dissected the spiral of the inner ear and found a ribbon of hair cells sitting on a membrane. Each responds to a different pitch, so the ear separates a chord into notes before the brain hears anything.

mean: Of the accessory smell organ in the nasal cavity of many animals
story: A Danish surgeon described a second smell organ tucked into the nasal cavity. In snakes and cats it reads chemical signals from other animals, which is why a snake flicks its tongue into the roof of its mouth.

mean: Of a pair of small lubricating glands near the vaginal opening
story: A Danish anatomist from a family of three generations of anatomists described a pair of pea-sized lubricating glands. His father named the lymphatic system's thoracic duct; the family put its surname on a remarkable amount of the body.

mean: Of a pair of small glands below the prostate
story: An English surgeon described a pair of pea-sized glands below the prostate. He also republished another anatomist's plates under his own name, causing one of the ugliest plagiarism rows in the history of anatomy.

mean: Of the duct draining the salivary gland under the jaw
story: An English physician who stayed in London through the plague of 1665 while most doctors fled described the duct draining the salivary gland under the jaw. The jelly that cushions the vessels inside an umbilical cord also carries his name.

mean: Of the duct draining the large salivary gland in front of the ear
story: A Danish anatomist found the duct draining the big salivary gland in front of the ear when he was twenty-two. He then left medicine, worked out how fossils form and how rock layers stack, and ended his life as a bishop.

mean: Of the clusters of hormone-producing cells scattered through the pancreas
story: A German medical student described strange islands of cells scattered through the pancreas and admitted he had no idea what they did. Forty years later they turned out to make insulin. He died of tuberculosis at forty-one.

mean: Of the ring of arteries supplying blood to the base of the brain
story: An English physician traced a ring of arteries at the base of the brain that lets blood reach it from more than one direction. If one vessel blocks, the ring can reroute around it, which is why some strokes cause far less damage than expected.

mean: Of the deep membranous layer of the abdominal wall
story: An Italian anatomist described the deep membranous sheet in the abdominal wall that limits how far leaked fluid can spread. He was so disliked that after his death a colleague kept his severed head on display in the university museum.

mean: Of the thickened band of tissue running from hip to groin
story: A French surgeon described the thickened cord of tissue running from the hip bone to the pubic bone. Every hernia repair works around it, and the two kinds of groin hernia are distinguished by which side of it they emerge.

mean: Of the ring of lymphoid tissue guarding the entrance to the throat
story: A German anatomist described the ring of tonsils and lymph tissue circling the entrance to the throat, catching whatever is breathed or swallowed. He also coined the words neuron and chromosome, which outlasted the ring in fame.

mean: Of the thin membrane separating two fluid chambers of the inner ear
story: A Baltic German anatomist described a membrane just two cells thick separating two fluid chambers of the cochlear spiral. The fluids on either side carry different salts, and that difference is what powers hearing.

mean: Of the thin membrane lying beneath the retina
story: A German anatomist described the thin layered membrane between the retina and its blood supply. It thickens with age and cracks, and those cracks are where the blood vessels of macular degeneration break through.

mean: Of the whorled cell bodies found in the thymus gland
story: An English microscopist described onion-like whorls of flattened cells buried in the thymus. He also used his microscope on London's drinking water, and his drawings of what lived in it helped force the city to build proper sewers.

mean: Of the granular protein-making bodies stained inside a nerve cell
story: A German neuropathologist invented a dye that turned the protein factories inside nerve cell bodies deep blue. When a nerve is injured the granules scatter and fade, so the stain became a way of reading damage directly.

mean: Of the giant motor neurons in the brain's movement cortex
story: A Ukrainian anatomist described the largest cells in the human cortex, giant neurons whose fibres run all the way down the spinal cord. Each one commands muscle directly, and a single cell can be a metre long.

mean: Of the regular gaps in a nerve's insulating sheath
story: A French histologist noticed that the insulation around a nerve fibre is not continuous but broken by regular tiny gaps. The signal leaps from gap to gap instead of crawling along, which makes a nerve impulse fifty times faster.

mean: Of the fibrous envelope surrounding the kidney
story: A Romanian surgeon described the fibrous envelope wrapping each kidney in its bed of fat. Surgeons still name the plane by him, because a tumour contained inside that envelope is a far better prospect than one that has broken out.

mean: Of the fascial layer lying between rectum and prostate
story: A French surgeon described a thin sheet of fascia separating the rectum from the prostate. Two centuries later it decides the outcome of prostate surgery: staying on the right side of that sheet is what spares the nerves.

mean: An Australian shrub with dense brush-like flower spikes
story: A wealthy young botanist paid his own way onto Cook's Endeavour and came home with fourteen hundred plants nobody in Europe had seen. He later ran Kew Gardens for four decades, and the bottlebrush-flowered shrub carries his name.

mean: A shrub with long spikes of flowers that attract butterflies
story: An English country rector spent his spare hours cataloguing mosses and grasses so carefully that Linnaeus later used his work. He never saw the shrub named for him: it came from China decades after his death, and now colonises railway sidings everywhere.

mean: A South American tree whose bark yields quinine
story: The bark of a Peruvian tree was the only cure for malaria for three centuries. Linnaeus named the genus after a vicereine said to have been saved by it, then misspelled her title. The story is probably invented; the spelling error certainly was not.

mean: A scented South African flower grown from a corm
story: A German botanist collecting in South Africa found a small scented flower on a one-sided spike and named it after a doctor friend back home. It became one of the most popular cut flowers in the world on the strength of its smell alone.

mean: A large brightly coloured daisy from South Africa
story: A German doctor ran a botanical garden in Moscow and explored the Volga collecting plants before dying at thirty-three. A colleague named a South African daisy after him, and it is now the fifth most sold cut flower on earth.

mean: A houseplant with large velvety bell-shaped flowers
story: A German botanist writing in the 1780s had a genus of velvet-flowered tropical plants named after him. Confusingly, the plant sold in shops under his name today belongs to a different genus entirely, which botanists have given up trying to correct.

mean: An Australian shrub with brush-like or spider-like flowers
story: A British collector who helped found the Royal Horticultural Society had a large Australian genus named after him. There are over three hundred and fifty species, from ground creepers to trees, and almost all of them are pollinated by birds rather than insects.

mean: A parasitic plant bearing the largest single flower on earth
story: The plant has no leaves, no stem and no roots. It lives inside a vine and erupts as a metre-wide reddish flower that smells of rotting meat to draw flies. It was named for the colonial official who founded Singapore.

mean: A fast-growing tree with large leaves and purple bell flowers
story: A German botanist working for the Dutch named a Japanese tree after the Russian grand duchess who had become Queen of the Netherlands. It grows faster than almost any hardwood, up to five metres in a single season.

mean: A low alpine plant with fleshy leaves and bright flowers
story: An American explorer crossing the Rockies collected a low plant with fleshy leaves whose root the local tribes ate. It survived being pressed, dried and carried across a continent, and then sprouted in a Philadelphia garden.

mean: A North American wildflower with fringed pink or purple petals
story: The other leader of the great American overland expedition got his name on a genus of showy pink wildflowers found along the route. His companion got a different plant, so the two men who crossed the continent together are commemorated in separate genera.

mean: A small creeping woodland plant with paired pink bell flowers
story: The man who named tens of thousands of species reserved one for himself, and pointedly chose a tiny creeping woodland plant with two nodding pink bells. A colleague wrote that it was lowly, insignificant and flowered only briefly, like its namesake.

mean: A garden shrub with trumpet-shaped pink or red flowers
story: A German chemistry professor who also taught botany had an East Asian flowering shrub named after him. Robert Fortune brought it out of China in the 1840s on the same journeys that smuggled tea plants to India.

mean: A showy tropical orchid with large frilled flowers
story: An English collector was sent a crate of Brazilian mosses packed in what looked like dead stems. He planted the packing material anyway. It flowered into an orchid nobody had seen, and the genus took his name.

mean: An evergreen shrub with clusters of cup-shaped flowers
story: Linnaeus sent a student to North America to find plants that might survive Swedish winters. He came back with an evergreen shrub whose stamens are spring-loaded and fling pollen at visiting bees. Linnaeus named it after him.

mean: The shrub whose leaves yield the reddish dye henna
story: A Scottish army physician paid the printing costs of the book in which Linnaeus first laid out his system of classification. In return Linnaeus named the henna shrub after him, so the dye on a thousand years of hands carries a Scot's surname.

mean: A carnivorous plant with tube-shaped leaves that trap insects
story: A French surgeon in Quebec sent European botanists a plant whose leaves form tall tubes half full of liquid. Insects walk in on downward-pointing hairs and cannot climb out. The genus was named after him.

mean: A thorny North American tree with hanging white flower clusters
story: A gardener to three French kings planted a North American tree in Paris around 1601. One of the specimens he or his son planted is still alive, propped on crutches, making it the oldest tree in the city.

mean: An air plant that takes moisture from the air rather than soil
story: A Finnish botanist was so violently seasick on one voyage that he walked home round the Gulf of Bothnia instead. Linnaeus, who found this funny, gave his name to a genus of plants that seem to repel water and live on air.

mean: The California poppy, with silky orange cup-shaped flowers
story: A Baltic German ship's surgeon sailed round the world twice on Russian expeditions. His friend and shipmate named the golden poppy of the Californian hills after him, saddling the state flower with one of the hardest genus names in botany.

mean: A low trailing rock plant with dense purple flowers
story: A French botanical artist who drew plants on expeditions to the Levant had a low cushion-forming rock plant named after him. It is the sheet of purple that spills over garden walls in April.

mean: A plant with enormous rhubarb-like leaves
story: A Norwegian bishop who catalogued his country's flora between sermons had a genus named after him whose largest species carries leaves three metres across, big enough to shelter under. Nothing in Norway grows remotely like it.

mean: A tall African plant with a spike of red and yellow tubular flowers
story: A German physician published books illustrated by pressing inked plants straight onto the page. A South African plant whose flower spike burns from red at the top to yellow at the bottom was later named after him.

mean: An aromatic North American herb, also called bergamot
story: A Spanish physician in Seville wrote the first European account of the plants coming back from the Americas, including tobacco and sunflowers, without ever crossing the Atlantic himself. Linnaeus named a fragrant mint-family herb after him.

mean: The African violet, a small houseplant with velvety leaves
story: A German administrator in East Africa found a small purple flower growing in the shade of a rock and posted seed home to his father. It became one of the most popular houseplants in the world, and the genus took the family name.

mean: An Antarctic seal that dives deeper and longer than any other
story: A British sealing captain pushed his ship further south than anyone before him through an unusually ice-free summer. The sea he found and the seal that lives in it both took his name; the seal can hold its breath for eighty minutes.

mean: The last surviving species of wild horse, native to the Mongolian steppe
story: A Russian explorer brought back a skull and hide from the Mongolian steppe that proved a genuinely wild horse still existed, never domesticated. It went extinct in the wild in the 1960s and was brought back from twelve captive animals.

mean: Describing several North Pacific animals recorded by one naturalist
story: A German naturalist got ten hours ashore in Alaska and used them so well that six species now carry his name. He described a nine-metre sea cow that was hunted to extinction within twenty-seven years of his sighting it.

A French explorer charting the Antarctic coast named the land he found after his wife, waiting at home in France. The small penguins nesting on it took the same name, so the commonest penguin in Antarctica is called after a Frenchwoman who never went there.

mean: A large sleek grey hunting dog with pale eyes
story: The court of a German grand duchy bred a grey gundog for hunting big game, then kept the bloodline closed to outsiders for a century. When Americans finally got some in the 1920s, the breed carried the duchy's name.

mean: A very large gentle dog bred for water rescue
story: Fishermen on a cold Canadian island bred an enormous dog with webbed feet and a waterproof coat to haul nets and pull drowning men out of the surf. One is recorded as having saved twenty people from a single wreck.

mean: A slender long-haired hunting hound of the Middle East
story: A slender hound bred to run down gazelle across open desert appears in Egyptian tomb paintings four thousand years old. Bedouin tribes let them sleep in the tent, an honour no other dog received, and their name traces to an Arabian town.

mean: The largest of the terrier breeds, with a wiry tan and black coat
story: Mill workers in a Yorkshire river valley crossed terriers with otterhounds to get a dog that could hunt on land and in water. It grew into the largest terrier of all, and served as a messenger dog in the trenches of the First World War.

mean: A short-haired cat with a distinctive ticked coat
story: A cat shown in London in 1871 was billed as having been brought back from an Ethiopian campaign. The claim is doubtful and the breed's real origins are probably Indian Ocean coastal, but the country's old name stuck to it.

mean: A genus of bacteria causing infections often caught from animal bites
story: The Frenchman who proved germs cause disease had a whole genus named after him: rod-shaped bacteria that live harmlessly in cats' and dogs' mouths and cause fast, angry infections in bitten humans.

mean: A genus of bacteria including the cause of whooping cough
story: A Belgian immunologist grew the whooping cough organism from his own infant son's cough in 1906. He won a Nobel Prize for separate work on how blood destroys bacteria, and the genus carries his name.

mean: A genus of paired bacteria including the causes of gonorrhoea and meningitis
story: A German bacteriologist aged twenty-four identified the coffee-bean-shaped paired bacteria behind one venereal disease, staining them from patients own samples. The same genus includes the organism that causes the most feared and fastest-moving form of bacterial meningitis.

mean: A genus of corkscrew-shaped bacteria including the cause of Lyme disease
story: A French bacteriologist gave his name to a genus of loosely coiled corkscrew bacteria. One species, carried by ticks that feed on deer and mice, causes Lyme disease and can hide in the body for years.

mean: A genus of waterborne bacteria causing a severe pneumonia
story: In 1976 a hundred and eighty delegates at a veterans' convention in Philadelphia fell ill and thirty-four died. It took six months to trace it to bacteria breeding in the hotel's cooling tower, and the organism took the delegates' name.

mean: A pear-shaped intestinal parasite causing persistent diarrhoea
story: A French zoologist had a pear-shaped single-celled parasite named after him. It clamps onto the lining of the small intestine with a sucking disc, and hikers who drink from clear mountain streams have been discovering it ever since.

mean: A genus of parasites spread by sandflies, causing skin and organ disease
story: A Scottish army pathologist found tiny bodies in the spleen of a soldier dead of a wasting Indian fever. The parasite is spread by sandflies, and in its worst form it destroys the liver and spleen and kills within two years.

mean: A genus of bacteria that live inside insect cells and alter their reproduction
story: An American pathologist gave his name to bacteria living inside the cells of most insect species on earth. They manipulate their hosts' reproduction so thoroughly that scientists now use them deliberately to stop mosquitoes carrying dengue.

mean: A genus of bacteria, one species of which produces a red pigment
story: An Italian pharmacist investigating why polenta turned blood-red overnight found a bacterium making a scarlet pigment, and named it after a countryman he thought had been cheated of credit for the steamboat. It is now a serious hospital infection.

mean: A genus of tick-borne bacteria that infect white blood cells
story: The German who invented chemotherapy and the first cure for syphilis had a genus of tick-borne bacteria named after him. They hide inside the very white blood cells sent to destroy them, which is why the infection is so hard to spot.

mean: A genus of branching soil bacteria causing lung and skin infection
story: A French veterinarian isolated a branching, thread-like bacterium from cattle on Guadeloupe. It lives in soil and dust and mostly troubles people whose immune systems are already failing, which is why it became far better known after 1980.

mean: A genus of tick-borne parasites that destroy red blood cells
story: A Romanian bacteriologist found parasites inside the red blood cells of cattle with a wasting fever. It was the first proof that a tick could carry disease, and the discovery reshaped how doctors thought about insects entirely.

mean: A genus of tick-borne parasites causing fatal cattle disease
story: A Swiss veterinarian who lost an arm in an accident became the founding figure of South African veterinary science. The tick-borne parasite named after him kills cattle across east and southern Africa, and shaped the whole continent's livestock trade.

mean: A genus of thread-like worms that block lymph vessels
story: A German physician working in Brazil found thread-like worm larvae in the urine of patients with grotesquely swollen limbs. The adult worms clog the lymph vessels, and the disease they cause still affects tens of millions of people.

Element ninety-six was made by bombarding plutonium with helium nuclei in 1944 and kept secret until the war ended. It was named for the husband-and-wife team who discovered radium, the only element honouring two people at once.

mean: A highly radioactive synthetic metal, element 99
story: Element ninety-nine was first found in the fallout of the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952. Its discovery stayed classified for three years, and it was named after the physicist whose equation had made such bombs conceivable.

Element one hundred appeared in the same hydrogen bomb debris as its neighbour. It was named after the physicist who built the first nuclear reactor under a Chicago squash court, and who had died the year before the name was announced.

Element one hundred and one was made one atom at a time, seventeen atoms in the first experiment. Naming it after the Russian who invented the periodic table was a deliberate Cold War gesture from an American team.

Element one hundred and four was claimed by both Soviet and American labs, and the two names fought it out for nearly thirty years. The winner honours the New Zealander who discovered that atoms have a dense nucleus at all.

Element one hundred and six was named after a living chemist, which caused a formal objection: no element had ever honoured someone still breathing. He had co-discovered ten elements himself, so the rule bent rather than held.

She worked out the theory of nuclear fission in exile after fleeing Nazi Germany, and her collaborator took the Nobel Prize alone. Element one hundred and nine was named for her decades later, an apology written into the periodic table.

Element one hundred and twelve was announced on the five hundred and thirty-seventh anniversary of the astronomer's birth. The team chose him to honour a scientist whose ideas took a century to be accepted and then changed everything.

mean: A silvery rare earth metal used in MRI contrast agents
story: A Finnish chemist analysed a black stone from a Swedish quarry and found an entirely new kind of earth in it. That single quarry eventually yielded eight elements, and both a mineral and this metal carry his name.

mean: A silvery rare earth metal used in powerful magnets
story: A Russian mining official who supplied specimens to chemists had a mineral named after him, and the element later teased out of that mineral inherited the name. He is the first person ever to have a chemical element named after him.

Element one hundred and two was claimed first by a Stockholm team whose result nobody could reproduce. The name they had chosen, honouring the founder of the prizes, survived even though their discovery did not.

Element one hundred and three was named for the physicist who invented the cyclotron, the machine that hurls particles fast enough to build new elements at all. Nearly every element past uranium exists because of his machine.

Element one hundred and seven honours the Dane who worked out that electrons sit in fixed shells. The team originally proposed a form of the name that would have been confused with boron, and had to be talked out of it.

mean: A radioactive metal used in household smoke detectors
story: Element ninety-five was named after a continent to mirror the element named for Europe directly above it in the table. It is the only synthetic element sitting in ordinary homes: a speck of it makes smoke detectors work.

Element ninety-eight was named for the state and the university where it was created. The team joked that they had skipped the tradition of honouring a person because getting to California had been hard enough for the pioneers.

Element ninety-seven was named for the university town where it was made, following the pattern of the element above it in the table, which had been named for a Swedish village. Both sit in the same column by design.

mean: A rare earth metal used in red phosphors and banknote security marks
story: A French chemist separated a new rare earth in 1901 and named it after his continent. It glows a distinctive red under ultraviolet light, which is why euro banknotes carry a trace of it as an anti-forgery mark.

A German chemist found a new element in a silver ore in 1886 and named it for his country. It filled a gap Mendeleev had predicted almost exactly, and its properties matched the prediction so closely that the periodic table was suddenly beyond argument.

A Polish-born chemist working in Paris isolated a new element and named it after her homeland, which at the time did not exist as an independent state. It was a deliberate political act disguised as a chemical one.

mean: An intensely reactive alkali metal, element 87
story: A French chemist found the last naturally occurring element to be discovered in 1939 and named it after her country. There is thought to be less than thirty grams of it in the entire earth's crust at any moment.

mean: A light silvery metal used in high-performance alloys
story: A Swedish chemist separated a new element from a Scandinavian mineral in 1879 and named it for the region. It turned out to be one of the elements Mendeleev had predicted and left a blank space for a decade earlier.

mean: A silvery metal used in phosphors and superconductors
story: One small quarry on a Swedish island produced a black mineral that turned out to contain eight new elements. Four of them were named after the village itself, which makes it the most honoured place name in the periodic table.

mean: A soft reactive metal that burns with a crimson flame
story: A mineral dug from lead mines in a Highland village turned out to contain a new element that burns crimson. It is the only chemical element named after a place in Scotland, and it is why fireworks can be red.

mean: A rock and mineral of calcium magnesium carbonate
story: A French geologist noticed that some Alpine limestone did not fizz in acid the way limestone should. It proved to be a different mineral entirely. Both the rock and the spectacular Italian mountain range made of it now carry his name.

mean: A yellow-brown iron oxide mineral, the main component of rust
story: Germany's greatest poet was also a serious mineral collector with eighteen thousand specimens. A mineralogist named the commonest iron oxide after him, so the substance that rust is mostly made of is named for the author of Faust.

mean: A zinc carbonate mineral, often banded and blue-green
story: An English chemist showed that two minerals long lumped together were chemically different. He never visited America, but left his entire fortune to found an institution there, and both the mineral and that institution carry his name.

mean: A calcium tungstate mineral, the chief ore of tungsten
story: A Swedish apothecary discovered oxygen, chlorine and several other elements, then largely lost the credit for each by publishing late. He had a habit of tasting his compounds, which probably killed him at forty-three.

mean: A white calcium silicate mineral occurring in needle-like crystals
story: An English chemist discovered palladium and rhodium, and made a fortune quietly selling purified platinum. A needle-crystalled calcium silicate was named after him, and the dark lines he first noticed in sunlight became the science of spectroscopy.

mean: A mineral whose crystal structure names a whole family of materials
story: A Russian mineralogist had one obscure titanium mineral named after him. Its crystal arrangement turned out to be shared by hundreds of compounds, and materials built on that pattern are now the great hope of cheap solar power.

mean: A gem that appears green in daylight and red under lamplight
story: A green gem found in the Urals was presented on the day the future tsar came of age. Under candlelight it turned raspberry red. Since those were the Russian imperial military colours, the stone became instantly fashionable.

mean: A pink or peach variety of beryl
story: A New York gemmologist persuaded a banker to fund the assembly of two of the finest gem collections in the world, both later given to museums. He named a newly recognised pink beryl after his patron.

mean: A pale pink or lilac gemstone variety of spodumene
story: A self-taught mineralogist joined Tiffany at twenty-three and became the most influential gem buyer alive. He described a pale lilac stone from California that fades in sunlight, and colleagues named it after him.

mean: A brilliant silicon carbide mineral used as a diamond substitute
story: A French chemist picking through fragments from a meteorite crater found crystals he first took for diamond. They were silicon carbide, almost unknown in nature. Grown in laboratories, they now outsparkle diamond and cost a tenth as much.

mean: A grey or brown aluminium silicate mineral of high-temperature rocks
story: An American chemist founded the journal that became the backbone of nineteenth-century American science and analysed the first meteorite fall studied in the United States. A high-temperature aluminium silicate was named after him.

mean: A volcanic rock that carries diamonds up from deep in the mantle
story: Diggers at a South African hill found diamonds in a strange bluish rock filling an ancient volcanic pipe. The rock had come up from a hundred and fifty kilometres down, fast enough that the carbon stayed diamond, and it took the town's name.

mean: A fine-grained volcanic rock of intermediate composition
story: The volcanoes running down the spine of South America erupt a rock midway between basalt and granite in composition. It was named for the range, and the boundary where that rock type appears around the Pacific carries the same name.

mean: The chief ore of aluminium, a reddish clay-like rock
story: A French geologist described a reddish rock near a Provencal village in 1821. It turned out to be the world's only economic source of aluminium, so every drinks can and aeroplane wing traces back to a name from southern France.

mean: Magnesium sulphate, used dissolved in baths
story: A farmer noticed his cattle would not drink from one spring on a Surrey common. The water was bitter with magnesium sulphate. Boiled down it became a famous purgative, and the town grew into a spa on the strength of it.

mean: Of the random jittering motion of tiny particles suspended in a fluid
story: A Scottish botanist watching pollen grains in water saw them jitter endlessly and could not explain it. Eighty years later Einstein showed the jittering was invisible water molecules knocking them about, which finally proved atoms are real.

mean: Of the blue glow emitted by particles exceeding light's speed in a medium
story: A Soviet physicist explained the eerie blue glow around nuclear reactor cores. Light slows down in water, so a particle can outrun it there, and the glow is the optical equivalent of a sonic boom.

mean: Of a junction where current tunnels between two superconductors
story: A Cambridge graduate student predicted that a supercurrent would tunnel straight through an insulating gap between two superconductors. Senior physicists doubted it. He was twenty-two, was proved right, and the effect now defines the standard volt.

mean: Of the voltage generated by a temperature difference across joined metals
story: A Baltic German physicist joined two different metals, heated one junction, and found a compass needle nearby swung. He had made electricity out of a temperature difference. Every thermocouple in every industrial furnace uses the effect.

mean: Of the heating or cooling produced by current across a junction of two metals
story: A French watchmaker who retired at thirty to do physics found the reverse of the thermoelectric effect: run a current through joined metals and one junction gets cold. Camping fridges and chip coolers run on it.

mean: Of the law that an induced current opposes the change causing it
story: A Baltic German physicist established that nature pushes back: a current induced by a changing magnetic field always flows so as to oppose that change. Drop a magnet down a copper pipe and it floats down slowly because of it.

mean: Of the two rules governing current and voltage around a circuit
story: A German physicist stated his two circuit rules while still a student: charge in equals charge out at any junction, and voltages round any loop sum to zero. He also co-founded spectroscopy and named the black body.

mean: Of the equation linking cell voltage to the concentrations of its reactants
story: A German chemist derived the equation linking an electrochemical cell's voltage to what is dissolved in it, then went on to state the third law of thermodynamics. Every nerve impulse in your body obeys his equation.

mean: Of the equation describing how reaction rate rises with temperature
story: A Swedish chemist nearly failed his doctorate for proposing that salts split into charged particles in water. He later won a Nobel Prize for it, and was the first person to calculate how carbon dioxide warms the planet.

mean: Of the law relating a solution's vapour pressure to its composition
story: A French chemist found that dissolving something in a liquid lowers how readily that liquid evaporates, in exact proportion to how much is dissolved. It is why the sea freezes later than a pond and why antifreeze works.

mean: Of the principle that a disturbed equilibrium shifts to oppose the disturbance
story: A French chemist stated that a chemical system at balance always shifts to undo whatever you do to it: squeeze it and it shrinks its own pressure, heat it and it absorbs heat. Industrial chemistry is largely the art of exploiting this.

mean: Of the series of visible spectral lines emitted by hydrogen
story: A Swiss schoolteacher with a taste for numerical puzzles found, at fifty-nine, a simple formula that fitted the four visible lines of glowing hydrogen exactly. He had no physical explanation. Bohr supplied one thirty years later.

mean: Of the weak attractive forces acting between neutral molecules
story: A Dutch schoolteacher who taught himself physics at night wrote an equation for real gases that accounted for molecules taking up space and pulling faintly on each other. Those faint pulls are why geckos can walk up glass.
